articles.body: Baltic Dry Bulk Freight Index Falls To Near One-Week Low in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 27/10/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s main sea freight index dropped on Monday, pressured by declining rates across the capesize and panamax vessel segments. The Baltic index, which measures shipping rates for capesize, panamax and supramax vessels, fell 32 points, or 1.23%, to 2,628 points. This marked the index’s lowest level in nearly a week. The capesize index decreased 65 points, or 1.71%, to 3,726 points, reaching a near one-week low. Average daily earnings for capesize vessels, which generally carry 150,000-ton cargoes of iron ore and coal, dropped by $585 to $30,292. Iron ore prices traded within a narrow range on Monday. Market participants balanced expectations of seasonally weaker demand in China, the world’s largest consumer, against possibilities of additional stimulus measures from Beijing to support the world’s second-largest economy. The panamax index declined 34 points, or 1.61%, to 2,075 points. This represented the segment’s lowest level since July 30. Source: Investing.com 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Shipping: The Car Shipping Trade Is in Full Effect
articles.summary: The car carrier business is rapidly growing with China, once again, at the center of this. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “China’s rapidly expanding automotive exports have emerged as a key driver of the Pure Car and Truck Carrier (PCTC) market in 2026, supporting vessel utilisation and...
articles.body: Shipping: The Car Shipping Trade Is in Full Effect in Hellenic Shipping News 27/10/2026 T he car carrier business is rapidly growing with China, once again, at the center of this. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “China’s rapidly expanding automotive exports have emerged as a key driver of the Pure Car and Truck Carrier (PCTC) market in 2026, supporting vessel utilisation and elevated charter earnings. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM), exports reached 8.205m vehicles in January-September, up 65.8% y-o-y, including 4.006m new-energy vehicles (NEVs). September alone saw 1.053m exports, of which 571,000 were NEVs, up 160% y-o-y. Meanwhile, domestic NEV sales contracted by 9.4% y-o-y, reinforcing manufacturers’ focus on overseas markets amid subdued domestic demand and intense price competition”. According to Intermodal’s Nikos Tagoulis, Head of Research Department, “behind this export expansion lies China’s highly integrated automotive supply chain, spanning mineral processing, battery production, electric motors and vehicle assembly. According to the IEA, China accounts for 91% of global refining of magnet-related rare earths, 94% of sintered permanent magnet production and over 80% of battery cell output. Rare-earth magnets are used in many EV motors, rather than in lithium-ion batteries themselves. Such dominance provides Chinese automakers with substantial economies of scale and cost advantages, while exposing overseas manufacturers to potential supply disruptions”. Source: Intermodal shipbrokers Mr. Tagoulis noted that “for the shipping sector, the implications extend beyond rising export volumes. Long-haul car shipments from China to Europe and Latin America generate considerable car-mile demand, while limited backhaul cargoes and Cape of Good Hope diversions prolong round voyages, tying up vessels and reducing effective fleet availability. Routing patterns are diverging, however, with some Chinese operators resuming Suez transits, while major European and Japanese operators continue to favour the Cape route. Against this backdrop, the 1-year time-charter rate for a 6,500-CEU PCTC climbed steadily through 2026 to approximately $95,000/day in September, 43% above its 2026 average and 21% above its 5-year average, returning to levels last seen nearly two years earlier”. “With extended voyages absorbing vessel capacity, Chinese exporters are also exploring alternative shipping solutions, creating supplementary opportunities for containerships and MPP units. Specialised racking systems allow two to four passenger cars to be secured inside a standard 40-foot container, depending on vehicle dimensions, for shipment through established liner networks. MPP vessels can alternatively carry vehicles on purpose-built flat racks. Illustrating this practice, COSCO arranged three containerised shipments totalling 13,052 vehicles from China to Europe during 2026. Nevertheless, these movements remain marginal, with minimal impact on containership and MPP tonnage demand”, Mr. Tagoulis added. Meanwhile, Intermodal’s analyst noted that “elevated PCTC earnings and tight vessel availability have prompted a substantial supply-side response. PCTC newbuilding contracts surged to 82 vessels in the first nine months of 2026, against just nine throughout 2025 and a 10-year annual average of 35. Consequently, the orderbook-to-fleet ratio stands at 26%, well above its historical average of 14%, raising concerns over future oversupply. However, with 64% of orderbook tonnage scheduled for delivery from 2028 onwards, much of the capacity expansion remains backloaded, limiting immediate supply pressure. Chinese automakers are also expanding their own shipping fleets, potentially reducing their reliance on the open charter market”. Source: Intermodal shipbrokers “Alongside the anticipated fleet expansion, European trade policy presents a further challenge to the demand outlook. In October 2026, the EU and China reportedly reached a preliminary understanding on proposed restrictions covering Chinese-built conventional and plug-in hybrid vehicles. Under the proposed four-year arrangement, potentially taking effect in December 2026, annual imports would initially be capped at 350,000 units, with the quota increasing by 6% each year, subject to formal implementation. Battery-electric vehicles would remain subject to separate EU anti-subsidy duties. Against projected Chinese hybrid imports of around 800,000 units in 2026, these measures could significantly constrain shipment growth along the China–Europe corridor. The impact on car-mile demand will largely depend on manufacturers’ ability to redirect exports to alternative markets or expand overseas production”, Mr. Tagoulis said. “Looking ahead, strong Chinese exports and extended voyages should continue to support PCTC earnings in the near term. However, accelerating vessel deliveries from 2028, potential Suez normalisation and growing trade barriers could gradually erode current market tightness. The key question is whether China’s export expansion generates additional global car-mile demand or merely displaces shipments from established producing countries. Ultimately, the outlook of the PCTC market will hinge on whether car-mile demand can keep pace with the anticipated fleet expansion”, Intermodal’s analyst concluded. Nikos Roussanoglou, Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide Tops 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Seafarer happiness slips as crews camaraderie props up failing shore-side support
articles.summary: Seafarer happiness has fallen for a third consecutive quarter, according to the latest Seafarers Happiness Index (SHI), published by The Mission to Seafarers with Inmarsat and Idwal. The Q3 2026 score of 6.81/10 is down from 6.87 in Q2 and 7.26 at the end of 2025. Six of the ten measures fell. Those linked to ...
articles.body: Seafarer happiness slips as crews camaraderie props up failing shore-side support in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 S eafarer happiness has fallen for a third consecutive quarter, according to the latest Seafarers Happiness Index (SHI), published by The Mission to Seafarers with Inmarsat and Idwal. The Q3 2026 score of 6.81/10 is down from 6.87 in Q2 and 7.26 at the end of 2025. Six of the ten measures fell. Those linked to life aboard improved, while those that depend on the ship–shore interface – connectivity, shore leave, wages and welfare ashore – all deteriorated. Interaction with fellow crew rose to 7.70, the highest-scoring measure, with seafarers repeatedly describing supportive crews as “family”. The report warns that this cohesion is increasingly absorbing failures elsewhere, and the industry risks mistaking that adaptability for acceptable working conditions. Shore leave remains the lowest-scoring measure, falling from 5.72 to 5.46, eroded by shorter port stays, remote terminals, security restrictions and minimum crewing. One respondent reported no shore leave across four consecutive contracts. Port calls that should offer recovery have become the most intense part of the voyage. “In port, we get slammed with dealing with various cargo, regulatory, and husbandry items, all while the office is pushing for the shortest turnaround time,” said one seafarer. Connectivity recorded the sharpest fall, from 7.46 to 6.89 – not because technology is failing, but because expectations have risen. Seafarers now ask whether access is affordable and reliable enough to support family life, with data caps forcing crews to ration calls home. Ben Bailey, Director of Programme, The Mission to Seafarers, said: “Seafarers are telling us that their crewmates are holding them together, and that should give us pause. Strong onboard relationships are something to celebrate, but they cannot be a substitute for proper support ashore. When shore leave disappears for contract after contract and calling home has to be rationed, we are asking crews to absorb problems the industry should be fixing. The resilience they are displaying is a clear warning.” Gert-Jan Panken, GM and Vice President, Inmarsat Maritime, said: “The latest Seafarers Happiness Index highlights the remarkable resilience of seafarers and the importance of strong relationships and community on board. It also provides valuable insights into where we, as an industry, can do more to enhance their experience at sea. Connectivity continues to play an important role in seafarer wellbeing, and expectations are evolving. Beyond providing internet access, the focus must be on delivering reliable, affordable connectivity that enables meaningful connections with family and friends. These findings are an important reminder of our shared responsibility to keep improving life at sea and supporting the people who keep global trade moving.“ Thom Herbert, Idwal’s Head of Global Strategic Accounts and part of the seafarer advocacy team, said: “When our surveyors walk a ship, the condition of the vessel and the wellbeing of its crew are rarely separate stories. A tired, overstretched crew cannot maintain a ship as it deserves. A poorly maintained ship makes every working day harder, more tiring and less safe. That’s why our grading looks at how a vessel is managed, not just its steel and machinery. This report shows crews holding things together through their commitment to each other. That should concern anyone with a stake in a ship. Crew welfare is not a soft issue alongside vessel condition. It is part of it.” The SHI is a quarterly survey conducted by The Mission to Seafarers, in partnership with Idwal and Inmarsat, providing vital insight into the lives and experiences of those working at sea. The full Q3 2026 Seafarers Happiness Index report is available here Source: The Mission to Seafarers Tops 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Iran Threatens the Hormuz Internet Cables: Four Gulf States Have No Subsea Route That Avoids the Strait
articles.summary: Iran Named the Cables Before Naming the Targets On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told a ceremony in Tehran that seven major internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and that new targets and new weapons would be unveiled. He added that this time the response would be much harsher. The statement...
articles.body: Iran Threatens the Hormuz Internet Cables: Four Gulf States Have No Subsea Route That Avoids the Strait in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 Iran Named the Cables Before Naming the Targets On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told a ceremony in Tehran that seven major internet cables run beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and that new targets and new weapons would be unveiled. He added that this time the response would be much harsher. The statement did not come out of nowhere. Earlier in October, Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Iran could strike U.S.-linked cables, data centers and AI facilities in a new war. In May, the IRGC said every cable crossing the strait could be placed under Iranian permits. The count is close to accurate. Six live cables cross the strait today. 2Africa, AAE-1, FALCON, GBI, Tata TGN-Gulf and OMRAN/EPEG. Two more, FIG and SEA-ME-WE 6, are under construction and due in 2027, which takes the total to eight. Iran’s figure of seven sits between the current and the near-future count, per TeleGeography data. The Cables That Cross the Strait • 2Africa: Gulf branch to Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Oman. Meta, Orange, Vodafone, China Mobile, center3, Telecom Egypt, WIOCC, Bayobab. • AAE-1: Qatar branch, UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia. Consortium including e&, Ooredoo, Zain, Omantel, Mobily, China Unicom, PCCW. • FALCON: Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman and Iran. FLAG. • Gulf Bridge International: Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman and Iran. • Tata TGN-Gulf: Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman. • OMRAN/EPEG: Oman at Khasab, Diba and Barka, and Iran. Zain Omantel, Vodafone. • FIG (under construction for 2027): Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman. Ooredoo. • SEA-ME-WE 6 (under construction for 2027): Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia. Four Countries Have Nowhere Else to Route Exposure is not evenly distributed, and the difference comes down to geography rather than cable count. Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar are the most exposed, because every cable they use lands inside the Gulf. All of their subsea traffic to the outside world has to pass through Hormuz. Iraq has three live cables, all landing at Al Faw. Kuwait has five, Bahrain five and Qatar seven, but FOG, Qatar-UAE and Kuwait-Iran never leave the Gulf. That leaves Kuwait with three routes out, Bahrain with four and Qatar with five. Iraq is building a land route from Al Faw to the Turkish border with Ooredoo. The UAE is better placed. Six cables land on its Gulf coast, but 14 land at Fujairah and Kalba on the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait though still within Iran’s reach. Oman has two cables at Khasab, 11 on its Gulf of Oman coast, and five at Salalah and Qalhat on the Arabian Sea. Saudi Arabia is the least exposed, with four cables at Al Khobar and 14 on the Red Sea at Jeddah, Yanbu, Duba and Haql. Even that is not immunity. Two Red Sea cables were cut near Jeddah in September 2025. Sanctioned Tankers Were Already Above the Cables The statement on October 19 followed vessel activity rather than preceding it. In the two weeks before Mohebbi spoke, Windward tracked two OFAC-sanctioned tankers linked to Iran drifting for days directly over regional cable corridors, both in ballast, both with no commercial reason to stop. The first was sanctioned by OFAC in September 2024 for moving cargo for Iran’s IRGC Quds Force. After idling off Khor Fakkan, it sailed to Muscat at 11 knots, slowed to under one knot at the cable corridors on September 30, and drifted for 73 hours before resuming speed and heading for Suez. Inside that window, the behavior is specific. It arrived under power, drifted at an average of 0.6 knots with the engine off, crossed the edges of the AAE-1, Bay of Bengal Gateway and 2Africa corridors, passed within half a nautical mile of FALCON, GBI and MENA, then left to the southeast at 10 to 11 knots. Four days before the drift, it had changed its MMSI, call sign, and flag code. EO imagery captured the vessel on station there on October 1 at 06:52 UTC, confirming its position independently of what it was broadcasting. The second vessel, sanctioned by OFAC in November 2025 for carrying Iranian LPG, was running from the Malacca Strait toward a transfer off Dubai. On October 4, it stopped in the central Arabian Sea, 660 nautical miles out, and loitered for 115 hours at a median of 0.6 knots. The drift crossed the AAE-1, FEA, SEACOM/TGN-Eurasia, IMEWE and SeaMeWe-4 routes in water roughly 3,700 meters deep. It was the longest drift recorded on that corridor since late May. Neither drift can be characterized as a confirmed survey. What can be said is narrower. Two sanctioned vessels with Iranian links, both empty, both with destinations already set, made multi-day stops over cable routes in the weeks before Iran publicly threatened those cables, and both resumed normal speed immediately afterward. Mapping does not require touching the seabed. A hull-mounted multibeam sonar covers a swath roughly 3.5 times the water depth, and deep-water systems built into a container can be fitted to a merchant vessel. Whether that happened here is not established. Cutting the Cables Would Cut Iran Too One constraint sits inside the threat. FALCON and GBI land in Iran, at Bandar Abbas and Bushehr. Cutting either would sever Iran’s own links alongside the Gulf states’. OMRAN/EPEG runs between Oman and Iran, with the same problem. That does not make the threat empty. It makes it selective. 2Africa and Tata TGN-Gulf do not land in Iran, and the two cables due in 2027 do not either. Any action that distinguishes between these systems would require knowing precisely where each one runs, which is what makes the loitering activity worth watching rather than dismissing. What to Watch Three things will indicate whether the threat is rhetoric or preparation. Further loitering by Iranian-linked vessels over Gulf and Arabian Sea cable corridors, particularly over systems that do not land in Iran. Progress on Iraq’s land route to Turkey, which is the only alternative any of the four exposed states is actively building. And whether the FIG and SEA-ME-WE 6 routes, both due in 2027 and both running through the same strait, are redesigned in response. The physical vulnerability is not new, and it is not fixable in the near term. What has changed is that it has been named publicly by the party best positioned to exploit it, and that vessels linked to that party were observed above the cables before the naming. Source: Windward 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: Shipowners and operators need to maintain close checks on fuel quality following a series of off-specification alerts at major bunkering ports, advises German testing specialist CM Technologies (CMT), warning that contaminated or unstable fuels can result in costly engine damage and vessel downtime. articles.body: Bunker Quality Alerts Prompt CΜΤ Concern Over Engine Damage And Repair Costs in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 S hipowners and operators need to maintain close checks on fuel quality following a series of off-specification alerts at major bunkering ports, advises German testing specialist CM Technologies (CMT), warning that contaminated or unstable fuels can result in costly engine damage and vessel downtime. The advisory follows reports of fuel quality problems at Antwerp, Rotterdam, Houston, Singapore, Hong Kong, Piraeus and other bunkering locations during the past six months, involving excessive catalytic fines, poor fuel stability, high sediment levels and low flash points. In part, the drop in fuel quality can be attributed to the supply chain disruption caused by the current geopolitical landscape and conflict, says David Fuhlbrügge, joint managing director, CM Technologies (CMT). “Although conflicts cannot be directly blamed for individual cases of contaminated or off-specification fuel, changes in the availability and sourcing of blending components are important factors shipmanagers need to consider when managing bunker quality,” he said. In August, fuel testing specialist VPS identified the Middle East conflict as a major factor behind both rising bunker prices and deteriorating fuel quality. It also issued 29 bunker alerts during the first seven months of 2026, with excessive catalytic fines and fuel stability problems accounting for 72% of them. Bunkering Operation: Fuel Tanker Truck Refueling Commercial Vessel at Port Terminal “With fuel supplies under pressure and ships taking bunkers from different ports and suppliers, crews need to be particularly careful about what is going into their tanks.” Data published by West P&I in September, covering fuel samples tested between April and September 2026, found technical off-specification rates for heavy fuel oil (HFO) of 46.2% in Antwerp, 41.4% in Norfolk, 38% in the Panama Canal region and 35.5% in Rotterdam. The same report identified elevated sulphur off-specification rates among very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) samples tested in Rotterdam and Antwerp, although the club cautioned that the sample populations were comparatively small. Fuhlbrügge said the findings reinforced the need for shipmanagers to remain vigilant over the quality of fuels taken onboard, irrespective of the bunkering location. “Fuel quality should never be taken for granted. The consequences of getting it wrong can be expensive, not only in terms of machinery repairs but also the time spent dealing with blocked filters, damaged components and interrupted operations,” he said. In July, alerts were also published concerning high abrasive content in HFO supplied in Houston and the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp region, severe fuel stability concerns in Piraeus, high sediment in Las Palmas and low flash point fuels in Hong Kong and Singapore. “Catalytic fines are particularly damaging if they are not adequately removed during fuel treatment. The abrasive particles can accelerate wear in fuel injection equipment, cylinder liners and piston rings, potentially shortening component life and increasing maintenance requirements,” said Fuhlbrügge. Fuhlbrügge said the risks did not necessarily end once a bunker delivery had passed its initial laboratory checks. “Shipowners need to know how the fuel will behave once it is onboard, particularly when different batches are stored or mixed. Two fuels may be stable individually but incompatible when combined. Finding that out after sludge has formed in the tanks can mean considerable cleaning work and avoidable expense.” The commercial consequences are reflected in claims data from marine insurer Gard, which handled more than 70 bunker-related claims between January and May 2026, an increase of 50% over the corresponding period last year. Almost all involved fuel quality, with some vessels disabled or requiring towage. Lloyd’s Register FOBAS has also suggested that fuels meeting routine ISO 8217 specifications can still cause operational problems, particularly where unusual blending components or poor compatibility affect fuel handling and treatment. CMT supplies onboard test equipment for checking fuel compatibility, catalytic fines, water content, viscosity and density. Its compatibility tester, for example, allows engineers to assess the behaviour of different fuel batches before mixing, while its other instruments provide additional checks on fuel condition. “Onboard testing complements independent laboratory analysis and established fuel management procedures,” said Fuhlbrügge. “With the cost of replacement parts, maintenance and lost operating time, preventing fuel-related machinery problems is considerably preferable to dealing with the consequences. “Crews need to remain alert to changes in fuel condition throughout storage, treatment and use. Bunkering may be a routine operation, but the quality of the fuel delivered should never be assumed.” Source: CM Technologies (CMT) Tops 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: The EU is showing how regional maritime rules can support a global framework at the IMO
articles.summary: In April 2025, governments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed on a historic global regulation, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way. Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions...
articles.body: The EU is showing how regional maritime rules can support a global framework at the IMO in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 In April 2025, governments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed on a historic global regulation, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way. Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan. If the current draft of the NZF were adopted, it would be a historic milestone in two key ways. Firstly, it would set common global targets for the world’s fleet to reduce carbon intensity of marine fuels. Secondly and more significantly, it could set the world’s first meaningful carbon pricing for a global industry. By collecting fees on any emissions that exceed agreed targets, it would raise $10-15 billion a year, providing financial support for clean fuels and for the sector’s transition in developing countries. Think investments in clean ports, zero-emission ships, and renewable energy production. If a ship reduces emissions enough to meet the targets, it would not have to pay at all. While T&E analysis has previously shown that the NZF in itself is not strong enough to reduce shipping emissions at the pace countries agreed to, the agreement set an important global standard for a sector so far exempt from most climate rules. The IMO’s failure to adopt the NZF as planned in October 2025 was a major upset not only for the industry, lacking the much-needed investment clarity and certainty, but also the world’s most vulnerable states who lack finance for their energy transition, while often facing the worst impacts from climate change. One of the leading arguments put forward by the NZF opponents, largely oil-producing states led by the US and Saudi Arabia, was that there are regional carbon pricing measures already in place, and adding a global regulation on top would burden the shipping industry twice-over. The EU’s carbon market, the EU ETS, which covers the EU’s share of shipping emissions on its trade routes, was identified by these countries as a barrier to agreement at IMO. The IMO is expected to discuss adoption of the NZF again in December 2026. But while the blockers are still failing to propose any meaningful compromise, the EU has since proposed important changes to the EU ETS for shipping, addressing the concerns and paving the way for global and regional regulation to co-exist and reinforce each other. There are three key signals sent out by the EU that should not go unnoticed by any government deciding on the future of the IMO NZF this year. 1. There will be no double pricing of emissions. The EU is clear that if the IMO establishes a carbon pricing scheme such as the NZF, a ship sailing internationally will not have to pay double for the same emissions under the EU ETS. T&E analysis shows that this overlap is already small, with only around 15% of relevant emissions covered by both ETS and NZF. The NZF would become more strict over time, gradually increasing its coverage. As it does, the ETS would need to adjust – at least until 2040, after which global targets are yet to be agreed upon. 2. Alignment, not backsliding. Given that the NZF is insufficient to meet the IMO’s own climate targets, coordinated regional efforts are needed to fill the gaps. Currently, the EU reports emissions from all routes to and from its ports, but charges only 50% of the emissions. The newly proposed “ETS as a service” would allow EU trade partners to raise revenues on their own 50% shares through the EU’s existing system, without the administrative burden of setting up their own ETS from scratch. 3. The ETS should support an equitable transition. Whereas all funds would previously be spent only in European projects, around €100 million per year is now due to be set aside to fund shipping decarbonisation in SIDS and LDCs. In addition, countries linked through “ETS as a service” could also receive subsidies for green investments, further encouraging bilateral cooperation. How would the two schemes interact in reality? Let’s take a ship in 2030, sailing from Tema, Ghana to Algeciras, Spain, emitting a total of 1080 tonnes of CO2 equivalent. Under the EU ETS, the vessel would be charged for 41% of its emissions. The NZF, due to its limited pricing mechanisms, charges no more than 23%. Due to their different scopes, only 9% of the total is liable under both policies. This is the source of the alleged concerns, and the share of emissions that would now be exempted under the revised EU ETS. Yet, to benefit from aligned rules, governments need to agree on a global deal first. As the IMO meets for what many expect to be a decisive round of discussions this November and December, some countries are aiming to weaken or delay the agreement, in order to protect their oil interests. Despite their efforts and many proposals to reduce targets, create loopholes, or prioritise unsustainable options like LNG and crop biofuels, the NZF is still on the table. Now, the EU is opening a path for its regional rules to co-exist with a global framework and involving others in the benefits. With the Commission having provided more clarity on how the ETS could co-exist with a global system, align with other regional measures and even provide some support to SIDS and LDCs, there is now even less justification for governments to use it as an excuse for weak action at a global level. Failing to adopt a robust framework would keep global shipping in its costly state of limbo, reliant on unreliable fossil fuels, while leaving the poorest countries even more vulnerable. Crucially, such an outcome would not exempt governments from their own climate obligations, at the IMO or otherwise. Source: European Federation for Transport and Environment 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan.
If the current draft of the NZF were adopted, it would be a historic milestone in two key ways.

articles.body: Shipowners urged to act as Bangladesh recycling prices surge, warns Wirana in International Shipping News 27/10/2026 Shipowners considering recycling older vessels have a narrow window to secure higher prices in Bangladesh, following an unexpected surge in offers despite continued weakness in the country’s domestic steel market, says Wirana Shipping. The oldest global vessel cash buyer has warned that the current price levels may prove short-lived, with limited vessel availability driving competition among recyclers and pushing offers beyond levels that can be sustained by underlying steel market conditions. According to Wirana’s latest weekly market report, a dry cargo vessel was sold for recycling in Bangladesh at approximately eight per cent above the previous week’s price levels. The increase comes despite sluggish domestic steel demand, with local mills remaining cautious about purchasing and stockpiling materials. Wirana believes similarly high prices may only be achievable for another three or four recycling candidates, creating a potentially valuable opportunity for shipowners already contemplating vessel disposals. Rakesh Khetan, CEO of Wirana Shipping, said: “What we are seeing in Bangladesh is an unusual situation where recycling prices are rising despite weak demand for steel. Recyclers are extremely keen to acquire vessels, but there are simply not enough candidates entering the market. “This competition is creating opportunities for shipowners to achieve prices that may not be available in the coming weeks. However, these levels are not supported by the underlying steel market, and we do not believe they can be sustained indefinitely.” Rakesh Khetan, CEO of Wirana Shipping Bangladesh’s recycling market has also experienced disruption from festival holidays, with trading taking place on just two days during the reporting week. Prices for local steel plates, local scrap and imported shredded scrap remained broadly unchanged. The wider international shipping market continues to restrict the availability of recycling candidates, with relatively strong charter earnings encouraging owners to keep older vessels trading rather than send them for demolition. Mr Khetan added: “Shipowners need to assess the commercial realities carefully. Waiting for prices to rise further could mean missing an opportunity that has been created by a temporary imbalance between supply and demand. For owners who have already decided to recycle, the coming days could offer particularly attractive conditions. Timing will be critical.” Source: Wirana Shipping Corporation 2026-10-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Port of Riga to test resilient maritime communications under new partnership
articles.summary: The Port of Riga is set to become a testing environment for resilient maritime communication technologies following a new partnership between port technical services provider LVR Flote and connectivity technology company HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory...
articles.body: The Port of Riga is set to become a testing environment for resilient maritime communication technologies following a new partnership between port technical services provider LVR Flote and connectivity technology company HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga on October 23, 2026, establishing a framework for developing and testing secure communication solutions designed to support critical port operations under both normal and disrupted conditions. The cooperation will focus on technologies capable of maintaining connectivity between vessels, sensors, vehicles, drones and port infrastructure, including situations where conventional commercial communication networks become unavailable. Under the agreement, the Port of Riga will serve as a real-world testing environment, allowing the partners to assess the performance of different communication technologies during actual port operations. The companies also intend to pursue joint research and development initiatives and explore opportunities to deploy successful solutions at other European ports. Developing resilient communications for port operations The partnership comes amid growing attention to the resilience of maritime infrastructure, particularly in the Baltic Sea region, where repeated Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference has affected shipping and port operations. HARDMODE develops communication systems that combine multiple technologies to reduce dependence on individual networks or infrastructure components. Its approach incorporates mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband communications into a unified system designed to maintain connectivity when individual technologies experience disruptions. According to the company, the architecture also relies on decentralised network nodes capable of communicating directly with one another while supporting the software required for specific operational applications. “Critical infrastructure is getting more demanding every year. As more sensors, vehicles and systems are connected, more of a port’s daily work stops when connectivity drops,” said Artūrs Lindenbergs, Founder and CEO of HARDMODE. Lindenbergs explained that the company’s approach combines multiple communication technologies with decentralised network architecture, allowing alternative connections to support operations when individual systems become unavailable. For LVR Flote, which provides technical services and supports infrastructure maintenance at the Port of Riga, the partnership offers an opportunity to assess these technologies against practical operational requirements. Potential applications include hydrographic surveys, infrastructure monitoring, navigation safety, maintenance activities and coordination between port stakeholders. “Port technical services have to keep running in everyday operations and in a crisis alike,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote. “Together with HARDMODE, we want to explore how hydrographic surveys, infrastructure maintenance and coordination with other port stakeholders could continue even when conventional networks are disrupted,” Ozoliņš added. Riga pilots could support wider European deployment Beyond the initial communication technology trials, the partners intend to establish an open testing framework involving other companies developing solutions for critical port infrastructure. This could include providers of monitoring systems, sensors, automation technologies and digital port services that depend on reliable data exchange. LVR Flote will contribute operational expertise and access to real port service requirements, enabling participating technology companies to evaluate their solutions in a working maritime environment. The cooperation also has an international dimension, reflecting HARDMODE’s connections with Latvia and the Netherlands. Both companies plan to explore joint international research and development initiatives, with the possibility of commercialising and expanding successful technologies into other European maritime markets. The partnership remains at the development and testing stage. The companies have not announced a commercial deployment contract, investment value or timetable for the introduction of the proposed systems into regular port operations.

The companies also intend to pursue joint research and development initiatives and explore opportunities to deploy successful solutions at other European ports.

articles.title: SAT-JAM: Ships must learn to navigate without GPS
articles.summary: A researcher in Denmark who has developed a new system for tracking satellite navigation interference from space has a stark warning for the shipping industry in today’s Maritime CEO interview: GPS can no longer be considered a dependable means of navigation. Kian Bostani Nezhad, a PhD researcher at the Technical...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Tech SAT-JAM: Ships must learn to navigate without GPS Splash October 27, 2026 0 0 2 minutes read A researcher in Denmark who has developed a new system for tracking satellite navigation interference from space has a stark warning for the shipping industry in today’s Maritime CEO interview: GPS can no longer be considered a dependable means of navigation. Kian Bostani Nezhad, a PhD researcher at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), believes the maritime industry needs a fundamental rethink of its reliance on satellite positioning. “GNSS interference has become a perpetual problem,” he tells Maritime CEO. “Everyone who uses GNSS must change their mindset from GNSS being a primary and dependable navigation solution, to it being a supplement to other navigation methods.” Nezhad is the creator of SAT-JAM, a freely accessible online platform launched in September that maps GNSS interference detected by satellites orbiting hundreds of kilometres above Earth. The project began with an unexpected conversation last year. “I heard a spacecraft operator complain about their spacecraft having problems with GNSS over Europe,” he recalls. Intrigued, Nezhad searched for publicly available navigation data collected by low-Earth-orbit satellites and discovered several European Space Agency missions providing the information. Every mission he examined showed evidence of interference. Nezhad then submitted a research abstract to the Advanced Maui Optical and Space Surveillance Technologies conference in March, before developing SAT-JAM, inspired by GPSJam, a website tracking interference experienced by aircraft. His findings demonstrate that disruption affecting ships in the Baltic, Black Sea and other maritime hotspots is not confined to the Earth’s surface. Satellites operating 400 to 600 km above the planet can also experience degraded positioning signals. The platform uses publicly available European Sentinel satellite data, updated as new observations become available, to identify where spacecraft experience interference. However, Nezhad stresses an important distinction between detecting interference and locating its source. “SAT-JAM does not show where GNSS interference originates from, but where spacecraft measure the GNSS interference,” he explains. “The actual source, and the measurement can be far apart, due to the high altitude of satellites.” The distinction matters for shipowners attempting to understand the geographical spread of jamming and spoofing. Satellite measurements cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence of interference affecting vessels directly beneath them. Nezhad’s research background also includes maritime surveillance. His master’s thesis explored applying facial recognition algorithms to satellite imagery to identify and re-identify individual ships. Asked what practical advice he would offer shipowners facing increasingly unreliable satellite navigation, Nezhad identifies two priorities. First, operators should keep pace with improvements in GNSS receiver technology, particularly controlled reception pattern antennas (CRPA), which can suppress interfering signals. His second recommendation is more fundamental – seafarers must learn to navigate without GNSS. “I know it is easier said than done, but GNSS interference has become a perpetual problem,” he stresses. Britain warned shipowners earlier this month that satellite navigation can no longer be relied upon in major shipping regions, urging crews to practise operating without GPS. New guidance from the Maritime and Coastguard Agency highlights growing jamming and spoofing threats across the Baltic, Black Sea, Middle East Gulf and East Asia, affecting everything from ECDIS and AIS to autopilots and port systems. Maritime intelligence firm Windward recorded an average of 5,131 daily jamming incidents during the third quarter. The MCA recommends regular navigation drills, alternative positioning methods and greater awareness of equipment vulnerabilities. articles.body: Seatrium and Keppel’s wholly owned subsidiary, RigCo, have agreed to complete four offshore drilling rigs. The construction work has an estimated total contract value of more than S$500 million. The companies announced the agreement on October 26, 2026. They will carry out the work under an existing master services arrangement. RigCo owns all four rigs, which remain unfinished. The units include a seventh-generation drillship, a harsh-environment jackup and two mid-water semisubmersibles. The latter are suitable for demanding offshore conditions, including those in Northwest Europe. The companies expect to deliver the drillship in 2027 and the jackup in 2028. However, they are still assessing construction plans for the two semisubmersibles. RigCo will fund the work using its existing cash reserves. Keppel moves forward with offshore rig completion programme The agreement supports Keppel’s wider plan to generate value from its unfinished offshore assets. In July 2026, the company announced a programme to progressively monetise up to ten legacy rigs through the Keppel Offshore Fund. Keppel manages the fund, while Apollo participates as a limited partner. Through the programme, RigCo aims to complete its unfinished units and prepare them for commercial deployment. Meanwhile, the companies see improving conditions in the offshore drilling market. Limited newbuilding activity over the past decade has restricted the supply of modern rigs. At the same time, older units continue to leave the global fleet. Keppel also expects demand for advanced drilling equipment to increase in the coming years. “The demand for deepwater and harsh environment rigs is expected to increase over the next several years, providing conducive conditions for new, long-term charters of premium rigs,” said Cindy Lim, Chief Executive Officer, Infrastructure at Keppel and Non-Executive Director of RigCo. According to Lim, RigCo has been working with customers to understand their requirements as the market tightens. The company sees the completion programme as an opportunity to turn unfinished assets into income-generating units. RigCo already owns six modern jackup rigs that have been delivered and leased to customers since 2022. The four units covered by the latest agreement represent its remaining unfinished assets. Seatrium expands offshore construction activities For Seatrium, the agreement adds a significant programme of offshore construction work. The Singapore-based company provides engineering services covering rig design, construction, upgrades and maintenance. Seatrium also has extensive experience in developing high-specification drilling equipment. According to the company, more than two-thirds of operational jackup rigs worldwide use its designs. “This award reflects our undisputed capabilities to deliver complex projects safely, efficiently and to the highest quality standards,” said William Gu, Executive Vice President of Seatrium Energy (Marketing). Gu added that Seatrium would use its engineering and construction capabilities to help RigCo complete the assets. One of the units involved is based on Seatrium’s jackup designs. Its N-Class design can operate in water depths of up to approximately 500 feet, making it suitable for demanding offshore environments. The latest agreement comes as both companies anticipate stronger demand for modern offshore rigs. However, the completion schedule remains partly open. While the estimated contract value covers work associated with all four units, the companies have confirmed expected delivery years for only two. Plans for the remaining semisubmersibles are still under assessment.

Photo: Incat Tasmania The world’s largest battery-electric ship has officially entered commercial service, marking a major milestone for the maritime industry and the growing use of electric propulsion in large passenger vessels. The 130-meter China Zorrilla , built by Australian shipbuilder Incat Tasmania for ferry operator Buquebus, completed its first commercial crossing between Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Colonia, Uruguay, on October 22. The high-speed catamaran can carry up to 2,100 passengers and 225 vehicles across the River Plate, operating entirely on battery power without the need for conventional marine engines. At the heart of the vessel is an energy storage system exceeding 40 megawatt-hours, made up of more than 250 tonnes of batteries. The system powers eight electrically driven waterjets, making China Zorrilla the largest battery-electric vessel ever constructed. The ship is supported by dedicated high-power charging infrastructure at terminals on both sides of the river, allowing its batteries to be recharged between crossings. The start of commercial service follows an official ceremony in Buenos Aires on October 21, attended by Incat Managing Director Craig Clifford, Buquebus representatives, and maritime authorities and government officials from Argentina and Uruguay. Incat Chairman Robert Clifford described the achievement as one of the proudest moments in the company’s history, and credited hundreds of workers at Incat’s Hobart shipyard with overcoming significant engineering challenges to deliver the vessel, which represents one of the most ambitious projects in the company’s history. “This ship proves that large, high-capacity commercial vessels can operate on electric power,” Clifford said. Beyond its size and technical capabilities, China Zorrilla also offers a different passenger experience. Without conventional diesel engines, the vessel operates with significantly less machinery noise and vibration, while producing no direct exhaust emissions during crossings. Craig Clifford, who traveled aboard the vessel during its maiden commercial voyage, said the difference was immediately noticeable. He noted that passengers aboard a vessel of this size would normally expect to hear and feel powerful engines operating beneath them, but that familiar noise and vibration are largely absent. The ferry also features extensive passenger amenities, including approximately 2,300 square meters of duty-free retail space. The project’s completion is particularly significant given its evolution during construction. Originally designed to use dual-fuel engines capable of burning diesel and liquefied natural gas, the vessel was ultimately redesigned for fully electric propulsion, requiring substantial engineering changes. Its entry into service demonstrates the growing potential for battery-electric technology in high-capacity ferry operations, particularly on fixed routes where shore-based charging infrastructure can support regular crossings. For Incat, the milestone is also part of a broader shift toward electric vessel construction. The Tasmanian shipbuilder is currently building three 129-meter battery-electric ferries for Danish operator Molslinjen, along with two 78-meter hybrid-electric vessels at its Hobart facility. With China Zorrilla now carrying paying passengers, the company has moved one of the maritime industry’s most ambitious electric vessel projects from the shipyard into everyday commercial operation. articles.title: Shipping cuts training when it needs it most
articles.summary: Irene Rosberg, who runs the Blue MBA at Copenhagen Business School, returns to Splash today. When business conditions become difficult, training is often one of the easiest budgets to cut. In shipping, that is becoming an increasingly dangerous habit. The industry is asking its people to understand decarbonisation,...
articles.body: Contributions Operations Shipping cuts training when it needs it most Splash October 27, 2026 0 63 3 minutes read DGMA DGMA Irene Rosberg, who runs the Blue MBA at Copenhagen Business School, returns to Splash today. When business conditions become difficult, training is often one of the easiest budgets to cut. In shipping, that is becoming an increasingly dangerous habit. The industry is asking its people to understand decarbonisation, artificial intelligence, cyber risk, increasingly complex regulation and geopolitical disruption, often all at the same time. Yet education and professional development can still be regarded as discretionary expenditure rather than part of a company’s ability to operate successfully. There is a contradiction here because shipping wants better leaders, more skilled seafarers and managers capable of making increasingly complex decisions, but those capabilities do not simply appear when they are needed. Today’s maritime leader must be commercially savvy and technologically literate. Executives need sufficient understanding of AI and digitalisation to question the information put in front of them rather than simply accept it. They need to understand cyber risk, regulation and decarbonisation while remaining capable of responding when geopolitical events suddenly alter routes, costs and commercial assumptions. Operational experience remains enormously valuable, but experience alone cannot prepare someone for every challenge now entering the industry. This is why I find the tendency to reduce training when companies come under financial pressure so short-sighted. Sometimes the lack of the right skills, knowledge or leadership capability may be contributing to the difficulty a business is experiencing in the first place. Cutting the investment that could address those weaknesses can make the problem worse. The same applies at every level of the industry. We rightly talk about training seafarers to handle new fuels, equipment and technology, but professional development cannot stop once somebody reaches shore management or the boardroom. Seniority should not exempt anyone from continuing to learn. If anything, the consequences of outdated knowledge become greater as responsibility increases. A chief executive does not need to become an AI engineer or a cyber specialist, just as a board member does not need to become an expert in every new fuel. They do, however, need enough understanding to challenge specialists, recognise risk and make informed decisions about issues that may determine the future of the company. That requires investment and shipping has historically placed considerable value on experience, and rightly so. But the speed of change means that what someone knew ten or even five years ago may no longer be sufficient for the decisions they face today. Lifelong learning cannot be a phrase we use in speeches while treating the training budget as expendable when margins tighten. Companies should also look carefully at what they mean when they say they cannot find the right talent. If the perfect candidate is expected to arrive with operational experience, commercial acumen, digital literacy, regulatory knowledge, leadership capability and an understanding of emerging technologies, perhaps the answer is not simply to keep searching. Perhaps companies need to build more of that capability themselves. That means identifying people with potential, exposing them to different areas of the business and continuing to educate them throughout their careers. It means developing seafarers for shore positions and managers for executive responsibility. It also means recognising that the future leaders of shipping may come from broader professional backgrounds than they did previously. Education should not simply prepare somebody for their next job. Done properly, it creates organisations that are better equipped to deal with the unexpected. That matters enormously in shipping because unpredictability has become part of everyday management. A geopolitical event can alter trading patterns overnight. A cyber incident can affect operations across a fleet. New regulation can change investment decisions, while AI can alter established ways of working faster than traditional training structures can respond. No company can predict every disruption. It can, however, decide whether it has people capable of understanding what is happening and responding intelligently. Human capital should therefore not be regarded as a cost to be cut when times are difficult. It is part of the infrastructure of a maritime business, every bit as important to resilience as technology, vessels and financial capacity. Shipping will spend enormous sums preparing its fleets for the future. It should be equally serious about preparing the people who will be expected to lead them. He added that the MSC ESG Recognition confirms the certified systems supporting the company’s sustainability priorities. It also provides stakeholders with greater transparency about how MSC manages these areas. Massimo Alvaro, Managing Director of Business Assurance Italy at DNV, said companies are placing greater emphasis on ESG-related risks and performance. “An ESG Recognition issued by DNV confirms which certified management systems a company is operating to support its ESG performance,” he noted.

REUTERS/Stringer Two new maritime security warnings issued Monday point to continued dangers for commercial shipping in the Middle East, with one tanker confirmed disabled by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and another vessel reportedly on fire in the northern Persian Gulf. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it received a verified, time-late report of a tanker struck by an unknown projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on October 23 at 0839 UTC. The impact disabled the vessel, although all crew members were reported safe. UKMTO did not identify the tanker or provide details about the extent of the damage. No assessment of possible environmental impacts was available. The incident was disclosed three days after it occurred, highlighting the continuing delays in reporting attacks against commercial vessels in the region. In a separate warning issued Monday , UKMTO said it had received multiple third-party reports of a vessel on fire approximately 63 nautical miles southeast of Al-Faw, Iraq, in the northern Persian Gulf. The vessel’s identity, crew status, extent of damage and potential environmental impact were unknown. UKMTO classified the report as suspicious activity rather than a confirmed attack. The cause of the fire remains unclear, and authorities are investigating. The two reports come amid continued attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, with violence increasingly extending into the wider Persian Gulf. In its latest advisory, issued October 25 , the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) maintained its SEVERE threat assessment for the Strait of Hormuz, warning that further deliberate attacks were highly likely. The assessment also kept the threat level across the wider Persian Gulf at SUBSTANTIAL , citing five attacks inside the Gulf since October 7, including incidents near anchorages and ship-to-ship transfer areas. JMIC reported 156 confirmed maritime security incidents across the region since March 1. That figure was published before UKMTO disclosed the latest verified tanker attack. The advisory highlighted another recent incident involving an LPG tanker struck by an unidentified projectile on October 22, approximately seven nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman. That vessel subsequently reached an anchorage off Khor Fakkan. According to JMIC, Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps activity continues to include attacks, attempted attacks, drone overflights, surveillance and radio communications directing commercial vessels toward Iranian-controlled routes. The latest incidents also underscore the growing risks beyond the Strait itself, particularly in the Persian Gulf, where ships waiting at anchor or conducting cargo transfers remain exposed. Despite efforts by the United States to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, commercial traffic remains well below historical levels. JMIC reported 101 U.S.-facilitated vessel transits between October 22 and 24, compared with a historical average of approximately 138 vessels per day in 2025. The figures use different reporting methodologies, with the U.S. tally covering assisted transits rather than all commercial movements. Separate tracking data showed only single-digit daily transits outside the U.S.-facilitated system. Congestion also remains severe. As of October 25, JMIC estimated approximately 492 vessels were waiting outside the Strait of Hormuz, with large concentrations near Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and other regional anchorages. The continuing disruption comes as U.S. forces enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports while attempting to maintain safe passage for other commercial shipping. JMIC warned that vessels using the Strait face persistent threats from projectile attacks, possible renewed mining activity and electronic navigation interference. UKMTO has advised vessels operating in the affected areas to exercise caution and report suspicious activity while investigations continue. articles.title: Hormuz Chaos Sparks Legal Showdown Over Global Tanker Pricing
articles.summary: Commodity trader Mercuria Energy Group accused the Baltic Exchange of continuing to publish the world’s benchmark oil tanker rate, despite distortions caused by the Iran war, because it feared losing business to a competitor.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Russia's shadow fleet vessels wait in the unofficial anchorage area in the Gulf of Finland near Vaindloo, Estonia April 10, 2026. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Bloomberg) — Commodity trader Mercuria Energy Group accused the Baltic Exchange of continuing to publish the world’s benchmark oil tanker rate, despite distortions caused by the Iran war, because it feared losing business to a competitor. Lawyers for Mercuria kicked off a London trial claiming that the Baltic Exchange should have suspended the benchmark rate after exports through the Strait of Hormuz were strangled by the conflict between the US, Israel and Iran. The Baltic Exchange said the commodity trader’s claim reflects “instability and opportunism.” Founded in 1774, the Baltic Exchange plays a central role in setting global shipping rates. It maintains it was still possible to put a price on the freight risk, and that it had consulted consistently with the market after the Iran war severely disrupted oil shipments through Hormuz. Flows have since recovered close to pre-war levels. In an April 14 call, a senior freight assessor described the risk of the benchmark being replaced by a competitor as “the overriding fear of what we do here,” according to a document given to the court by Mercuria’s lawyers before the hearing on Monday. Mercuria also gave examples of tanker market participants, including the Baltic Exchange’s own staff, who called into question the continued publication of a rate for the route. The trading house said that the Baltic Exchange’s freight assessor didn’t submit a value into the company’s internal system that’s supposed to represent his personal view of where the index will be. When he did eventually submit a value, it included comments such as “doesn’t make any sense to shed an opinion on this route — crazy that we have to!” The case calls into question a pricing tool that until the Iran war acted as the benchmark for oil tanker earnings across the globe. The key TD3C rate underpins contracts between tanker owners and their customers as well as billions of dollars in derivatives. It’s based on the cost of hiring a supertanker from Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura, inside the Persian Gulf, to China, and also serves as a reference point for other routes. The Baltic Exchange is confident that it has met all its statutory, contractual and regulatory obligations in the production of the TD3C benchmark, Chief Executive Officer Mark Jackson said in a statement. The claim from Mercuria is “without merit,” he added. Mercuria has “huge index-linked exposures, which it has failed to risk manage,” lawyers for the Baltic Exchange said. After being caught out by the sharp rises in the benchmark, Mercuria “wishes to unseat TD3C, and it is reaching for any available argument to do so,” they added. Mercuria’s lawyers said the evidence showed the Baltic Exchange did not suspend the index because it wanted to keep the market for certain freight agreements active, and to avoid the risk of being replaced by a rival. One of the brokers who contribute to the index said on April 2 that it was “utter nonsense” to provide an assessment of the TD3C benchmark, given the unprecedented levels of disruption to traffic through Hormuz, according to another transcript presented by Mercuria. Mercuria is urging the court to declare that the Baltic Exchange breached its obligations and ought to have suspended the TD3C route. Lawyers for the Baltic Exchange said the risk of being replaced by a rival provider did not drive its decision making. The lawyers said passage through Hormuz was still possible. “The Baltic’s decision to continue publishing TD3C, was a decision which was not taken lightly,” lawyers for exchange said in a court document countering Mercuria’s allegations. The Iran war threw global commodity markets into turmoil by slashing shipments through Hormuz, which Tehran declared closed in the early days of the conflict. In recent months, volumes have recovered, with most trackers seeing shipments close to pre-war levels. A spokesperson for Mercuria didn’t immediately respond to an email for comment. Mercuria initially said it had incurred losses estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of US dollars as a result of the Baltic Exchange continuing to publish the index, but removed any estimate of financial losses from its most recent claim. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Singapore Yards Chase Profit From Europe’s Offshore Wind Push
articles.summary: At a shipyard in northern Singapore, a yellow platform towers over a maze of scaffolding and cranes. Resembling a 15-story building, the piece will be shipped halfway around the world to Europe to be installed into an offshore wind farm.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy U.S. Department of Energy (Bloomberg) — At a shipyard in northern Singapore, a yellow platform towers over a maze of scaffolding and cranes. Resembling a 15-story building, the piece will be shipped halfway around the world to Europe to be installed into an offshore wind farm. The 30,000-ton platform, known as a high-voltage direct current converter, is scheduled to leave Seatrium Ltd.’s yard for the North Sea in 2028, where it will sit 60 kilometers offshore and help transmit electricity generated by wind turbines back to land. It’s the latest effort by Singapore to tap into Europe’s green push. Singapore is repurposing expertise built over decades serving the largest offshore oil and gas companies for the energy transition. One of the biggest opportunities is exporting these enormous converters — known as HVDC platforms — to Europe, where the technology is widely used to transmit offshore wind power over long distances. The specialized technology is one bright spot in an otherwise battered offshore wind industry. Investment plummeted 72% year-on-year globally to about $12 billion in the first half of 2026, according to BloombergNEF. Yet few yards have the expertise and capacity to build the platforms, threatening a supply bottleneck as the European Union pushes ahead with plans to expand capacity. Seatrium’s platforms, each designed to handle about 2 gigawatts of electricity, are the largest of their kind in the world. It takes five years to construct one platform, which will operate for 40 years. GE Vernova Inc. supplies the HVDC technology in the platforms. The city-state and nearby islands now account for up to 20% of global capacity outside of China for the platforms, according to Ember analyst Lam Pham, up from a negligible share just a few years ago. Demand is poised to rise as Europe builds wind farms further out to sea, giving the region’s shipyards an opportunity to capture more of the business. “The country has invested, the company has invested — and this is a showcase of what is possible,” said Chris Ong, chief executive officer of Seatrium. Seatrium, which is partly owned by Singapore state investor Temasek Holdings Pte, was tapped by European grid operator TenneT Holding BV to build four platforms for North Sea clusters. About 7,000 workers will build the structures at yards in Singapore and Batam, an Indonesian island that’s 50 minutes away by ferry. Each platform, along with connecting infrastructure, costs as much as €5 billion ($5.6 billion) each, according to TenneT. Such platforms will be critical to unlocking growth in the global offshore wind industry, which faces challenges including high costs, supply chain shortages and regulatory hurdles. Despite these hurdles, Europe is still pressing ahead with a massive expansion of offshore wind to meet ambitious green energy goals. The UK awarded a record 8.2 gigawatts of capacity in its latest subsidy auction, while Germany and the Netherlands are implementing new revenue-protection mechanisms. With enough state support, BNEF expects installations to double by the end of the decade, led by China, UK and Germany. Singapore is now trying to position itself as the top choice for European developers. Rival yards in the Middle East are upended by the regional conflict; China and South Korea are mostly meeting domestic demand; and Europe’s shipyards are being taken up for building defence-related vessels. “Singapore would make it cheaper, even including the higher shipping costs, because the industry is very labor-intensive and labor costs in Europe are super high,” said Ember’s Lam. While wind turbines generate alternating current electricity, offshore developers use HVDC platforms to convert that power to direct current, allowing it to travel longer distances with less energy loss along the way. This will become a growing trend as wind farms move further from crowded shores. Ong – who was CEO of oil rig-builder Keppel Offshore & Marine before it was merged with Sembcorp Marine to form Seatrium in 2023 – is hoping to capitalize on offshore wind demand over the next two years. The company was chasing S$9 billion ($7 billion) worth of HVDC and HVAC projects across Europe and Asia Pacific as of July. Clean energy-related contracts currently make up about 40% of the company’s order book. In the yard in Singapore, the future of offshore wind power is slowly taking shape, with welders hunched over steel panels, piecing together the massive yellow structure one module at a time. For Ong, the demand for this infrastructure is not only being driven by the energy transition — it is part of Europe’s effort to secure future power supply. “The scale and the massive need for offshore wind is a big security drive,” he said. “It has to happen.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: Tianjin Port Holdings sets terms for two terminal acquisitions
articles.summary: Tianjin Port Holdings has agreed the financial terms for its proposed acquisition of two terminal operators from Tianjin Port Group. The transaction covers Tianjin Port Second Container Terminal Co. and Tianjin Port Huisheng Terminal Co. The two businesses operate container, general cargo and bulk facilities at the...
articles.body: Tianjin Port Holdings has agreed the financial terms for its proposed acquisition of two terminal operators from Tianjin Port Group. The transaction covers Tianjin Port Second Container Terminal Co. and Tianjin Port Huisheng Terminal Co. The two businesses operate container, general cargo and bulk facilities at the Port of Tianjin. Tianjin Port Holdings will acquire the entire equity interest in both companies. The total consideration has been set at RMB6.22 billion. Transaction structure The company will complete the Tianjin Port acquisition entirely through the issuance of new shares. No cash payment or additional financing will be required. Tianjin Port Holdings will issue 1,344,215,896 shares to Tianjin Port Group. The agreed issue price is RMB4.63 per share, up from the preliminary price of RMB4.36. Target company Business Transaction value Tianjin Port Second Container Terminal Container handling, storage and port services RMB3.86 billion Tianjin Port Huisheng Terminal General and bulk cargo handling, storage and transshipment RMB2.36 billion Total RMB6.22 billion The transaction value reflects independent valuations dated 13 October 2026. Container terminal included in the deal Tianjin Port Second Container Terminal provides container handling, storage, inspection and ship shore-power services. The company operates under a “Smart+Green” model focused on efficient and lower-carbon terminal operations. According to the announcement, its facilities can support round-the-clock operations involving the world’s largest container vessels. The container terminal reported revenue of RMB469.48 million for the first half of 2026. Its net profit after tax reached RMB186.27 million during the same period. Huisheng Terminal handles general and bulk cargo. Its facilities include two 100,000-tonne-class berths and two 150,000-tonne-class berths. Ownership interest will decline Tianjin Port Development Holdings currently owns 56.81% of Tianjin Port Holdings indirectly. Following the share issuance, that interest is expected to decline to 38.79%. However, Tianjin Port Development expects to retain control through an acting-in-concert agreement involving Grand Point Investment and Tianjin Port Group. Therefore, Tianjin Port Holdings would remain its subsidiary. Once completed, the two acquired terminal companies would become wholly owned subsidiaries of Tianjin Port Holdings. Their accounts would also be consolidated into the wider group’s financial statements. Completion remains conditional The transaction qualifies as a very substantial acquisition, very substantial disposal and connected transaction under Hong Kong listing rules. It remains subject to several conditions. These include regulatory registration, state-owned asset approvals and approval from independent shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting. Tianjin Port Development expects to issue a shareholder circular containing further transaction details by 25 November 2026. The company warned that the conditions may not be satisfied. Therefore, the proposed Tianjin Port acquisition may or may not proceed.

October 26, 2026 © Saildrone © Saildrone Saildrone announced a year-long mission with the Swedish Armed Forces to deliver persistent maritime domain awareness across Sweden’s territorial waters and exclusive economic zone in the Baltic Sea. Under the agreement, Saildrone will deploy and operate four Voyager unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) for 360 days each, representing 1,440 contracted vehicle-days of continuous maritime security operations. The 12-month commitment highlights a shift toward long-term operational capabilities, with the Swedish Armed Forces securing a full year of persistent maritime domain awareness to safeguard critical waters from the outset. NORDEFCO is a cooperative organization that unites Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and other Northern European countries to streamline defense cooperation and field proven regional security solutions. The Saildrone Voyager fleet will continuously patrol Sweden’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea, delivering real-time maritime intelligence directly to the Swedish Armed Forces. Operating as a managed service, Saildrone maintains, deploys, and tasks the USVs, enabling Sweden to maintain persistent maritime domain awareness without deploying additional crewed ships. Saildrone also recently registered four Saildrone Voyager USVs in Denmark to operate under the Danish national flag. The registration establishes a clear flag-state framework for Saildrone USVs operating internationally and supports the company operating alongside various European nations.
