articles.title: Middle East Officials Meet Discuss Deescalation Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks
articles.summary: Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the…
articles.body: Middle East Officials Meet Discuss Deescalation Amidst Continued Houthi Attacks Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © mykhailo - stock.adobe.com Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom. The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations — which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August — since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". Saudi Arabia was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said. Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meeting. Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. Qatari mediators were in Tehranon Sunday, an official told Reuters. Earlier efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June but fighting between Iran and the United States soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front. US AND IRAN THREATEN NEW ATTACKS The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, pushed up global oil and gas prices, left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new humanitarian crisis in Yemen. Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran. Iranian security officials have told Reuters that Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again. The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese Hezbollah militia, has eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections that decide control of Congress. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's discussions would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran". Baghaei said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus of Monday's meeting was to build a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, the official said. An Iranian official said there would be no discussion of Iran's nuclear programme at Monday's meeting and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met. Those conditions include ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance has said Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. Pakistan's military media office and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. PARLIAMENT APPROVES EGYPTIAN DEFENCE SUPPORT FOR SAUDIS Saudi Arabia has ⁠intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, ports and oil installations. On Monday, the Houthis said they had ‌attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had resumed operations at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks. The parliament in Egypt, which is not a signatory to the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia, a major financial and political partner for Cairo. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement says signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters. The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia. Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week. (Reuters)

October 26, 2026 © Adobe Stock/chakisatelier Oil prices fell $2 a barrel on Monday amid hopes of easing hostilities between the United States and Iran, but persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept investors wary and prices near six-month highs. Brent crude futures were down $2.03, or 1.7%, at $114.70 at 10:37 a.m. ET (1437 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $2.60, or 2.5%, at $100.71 per barrel. On Friday, prices settled more than $3 higher, with Brent finishing the week up 6% and WTI ending the week 2.3% higher. "With the jeopardy doubled by Houthi attacks into Saudi, any Brent price dips back to the lows of last week will find grateful buyers," PVM Oil Associates analyst John Evans said. "Corrective processes are notoriously difficult to quantify, but this one has nowhere near reached any sort of levels where bulls might abandon hope," he said. Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations. IRAN WAR MEDIATION EFFORTS RESUME On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said. Despite the mediation talks, attacks continued over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had struck pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West crude oil pipeline and Riyadh airport. Saudi Arabia said on Sunday it had intercepted more missiles and drones. The effects of the US-Israeli war with Iran that began on February 28 continue to reverberate as companies adjust to the disruptions of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait caused by the conflict. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, a think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. An oil spill from a strike-damaged tanker off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has widened, satellite images showed, triggering more beach closures and raising environmental concerns. articles.summary: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections.

REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo By Ron Bousso LONDON, Oct 24 (Reuters) – When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, “energy dominance” was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections. Ironically, it was the US position as the world’s top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country’s onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to “unleash American energy”, prioritizing oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the Arctic territory. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after Washington removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently took control of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude LCOc1 peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record $145 reached in 2008, when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington’s Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unraveled longstanding supply routes and sent shipping prices skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while diesel surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including easing biofuel blending mandates and, most controversially, reaching a diesel supply agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a diesel export ban, officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centers underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly many in Asia, the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had balked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Horizon Maritime The Louisiana-based Chouest Group has acquired Canadian marine and offshore services provider Horizon Maritime, expanding its presence across Canada’s East and West coasts and into the Arctic. The deal, announced Monday, brings together Chouest’s global offshore support fleet, subsea capabilities, shipbuilding operations and marine technology businesses with Horizon Maritime’s established Canadian operations and expertise in harsh-environment offshore services. Horizon Maritime, based in St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, was acquired from CFFI and its lender, HPS, through a strategic partnership with the company’s founders. Financial terms were not disclosed. The acquisition gives Chouest a stronger foothold in Canada’s offshore energy, Arctic and marine sectors, while providing Horizon access to a much larger fleet and range of specialized services. “We are excited to welcome Horizon Maritime to the Chouest Group,” said Dino Chouest. “We see immense value in Horizon’s team, leadership and operational excellence.” “Combining Chouest’s global fleet expertise and technology with Horizon’s local footprint across Canada’s vast coastlines opens up incredible growth potential across Canada’s East Coast, West Coast and Arctic regions,” he added. Horizon Maritime specializes in marine operations in challenging environments, with experience supporting offshore energy projects, Arctic operations and other specialized maritime activities. The company has also developed relationships with Indigenous communities and organizations across Canada. Under the agreement, Horizon will retain its existing management team and leadership structure. Steve Widmeyer will continue as CEO, while Widmeyer and co-founder Sean Leet will join the company’s board of directors. The companies said the arrangement will ensure continuity for existing customers, ongoing projects and crewing operations while opening the door to expanded services across the country. For Horizon, the deal also comes as Canada looks to strengthen its maritime capabilities, particularly in the Arctic, where commercial activity, infrastructure development and national security interests are increasingly overlapping. “This is an opportunity to build on what we have created and take Horizon Maritime into its next phase of growth,” said Leet. “The Chouest Group brings significant marine experience, assets and capabilities that will help us scale Horizon Maritime’s offerings to provide increased services and support to our valued customers, while increasing dual-use capacity at a key moment in time for our region and our country.” Widmeyer emphasized the opportunities the partnership creates for Horizon’s employees, including career development and long-term growth. The companies also said they remain committed to expanding Indigenous participation in Canada’s marine economy. The acquisition extends the reach of the privately held, family-owned Chouest Group, which operates across offshore vessel ownership and operations, shipbuilding, subsea services, specialized engineering and advanced technology manufacturing. For Horizon Maritime, the combination provides access to Chouest’s global resources while maintaining its Canadian management and established customer relationships. articles.title: Port of Santos begins regular ethanol bunkering operations
articles.summary: CMA CGM, Copersucar, Bunker One and the Santos Port Authority have launched regular ethanol bunkering operations at the Port of Santos in Brazil. The first operation under the programme took place on 19 October 2026. It involved the 13,000 TEU containership CMA CGM Iron. The vessel features the Everllence-B&W...
articles.body: CMA CGM, Copersucar, Bunker One and the Santos Port Authority have launched regular ethanol bunkering operations at the Port of Santos in Brazil. The first operation under the programme took place on 19 October 2026. It involved the 13,000 TEU containership CMA CGM Iron . The vessel features the Everllence-B&W G95ME-C10.5-LGIM engine. According to the project partners, it is the world’s first certified tri-fuel marine engine capable of operating with ethanol. The operation moves ethanol bunkering at Santos from an initial trial to a regular commercial supply model. Further deliveries to CMA CGM vessels are planned before the end of 2026. Ethanol supply chain at Santos Copersucar supplies the ethanol through its established and certified production chain. Evolua Etanol transports the fuel from Copersucar’s associated mills to the Port of Santos. AGEO Terminais stores the ethanol at the port. Bunker One then manages the bunkering operation at the Santos Brasil terminal. Bunker One developed a dedicated protocol for the operation after several months of preparation and staff training. The process considers ethanol’s low flash point and the specific safety requirements associated with its handling. “The operation demonstrates that ethanol can be incorporated into maritime activities safely, reliably and at commercial scale,” said Giovani Grassi, CEO of CMA CGM Brazil. He added that the initiative supports CMA CGM’s efforts to introduce fuels with lower carbon intensity and develop new energy supply chains for shipping. New maritime market for Brazilian ethanol Copersucar described the programme as the beginning of the world’s first maritime ethanol bunkering corridor. “This marks a milestone for ethanol and shipping,” said Tomás Manzano, President of Copersucar. “It opens a new global destination market for the fuel.” According to Manzano, the programme connects Brazil’s production and logistics capabilities with international demand for maritime decarbonisation. The partners said global marine fuel consumption exceeds 270 billion litres annually. Based on energy equivalence, replacing 10% of that consumption could create additional demand for around 50 billion litres of ethanol per year. Alternative-fuel fleet continues to expand The project partners also pointed to the growing number of vessels equipped with alternative-fuel engines. Citing DNV data, they said 159 vessels currently operate with methanol-capable engines that can also use ethanol. More than 450 additional vessels with this technology are scheduled for delivery by 2030. Flavio Ribeiro, CEO of Bunker One Latin America, said the initiative combines Brazil’s ethanol production capacity with Bunker One’s international marine fuel network. Anderson Pomini, President of the Santos Port Authority, described the operation as a step towards a new phase of sustainable port and maritime development.

The first operation under the programme took place on 19 October 2026.

REUTERS/Loren Elliott A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers is warning major banks and port authorities against facilitating Russian diesel shipments under President Donald Trump’s controversial agreement with Vladimir Putin, raising the prospect of legal action and congressional investigations as tankers carrying Russian fuel begin heading toward American ports. In an October 24 letter , lawmakers called on six major financial institutions and port authorities in Texas and New York to preserve records related to Russian diesel transactions, including shipping documents, vessel records, contracts and communications with government officials. The letter, first reported by Axios , warns that importing Russian diesel into the United States raises serious legal questions and could expose companies involved in the trade to future investigations. The warning was sent to JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, as well as port authorities overseeing Houston, Beaumont, Corpus Christi and the Port of New York and New Jersey. Lawmakers urged the institutions not to participate in the purchase, transportation, importation, unloading, storage, financing or distribution of Russian-origin diesel in the United States. They also called on the companies to avoid facilitating shipments to other international markets under the administration’s temporary sanctions relief. The effort was led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and signed by Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), along with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.). Several of the Democratic signatories could lead powerful congressional committees if their party wins control of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. The lawmakers requested confirmation by October 28 that relevant records are being preserved, including shipping documents, contracts and communications related to Russian diesel transactions. The warning comes as the first Russian diesel shipments approach the United States following Trump’s October 9 agreement with Moscow, which temporarily eased sanctions in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. As gCaptain reported, the Vietnamese-flagged tanker PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), carrying approximately 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, is signaling Norfolk, Virginia, as its destination, with an expected arrival on November 2. Another tanker, the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, loaded approximately 40,000 metric tons of diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. Reuters reported the vessel was signaling New York, with an estimated arrival on November 7. Neither shipment has been confirmed as destined for a U.S. buyer. Under the agreement, Russia committed to supplying an initial 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter. The Treasury Department subsequently issued General License 135, authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. But lawmakers argue the arrangement conflicts with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibited imports of Russian petroleum products following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. They contend that the administration cannot simply waive those statutory restrictions. The Treasury Department maintains that the agreement is legal, while the White House has defended the move as necessary to ease energy costs amid severe market disruptions caused by the war with Iran. For the maritime industry, the dispute adds uncertainty to a trade Washington has just moved to reopen. Shipowners, charterers, insurers, banks and terminal operators now face the prospect of facilitating shipments that lawmakers are already threatening to investigate. articles.title: C.H. Robinson expands AI automation across ocean and air freight
articles.summary: C.H. Robinson has introduced new artificial intelligence capabilities for ocean shipping, air freight and customs brokerage, expanding its Lean AI technology into global freight forwarding operations. The development, announced on October 26, 2026, introduces specialised AI agents capable of handling complex shipping...
articles.body: C.H. Robinson has introduced new artificial intelligence capabilities for ocean shipping, air freight and customs brokerage, expanding its Lean AI technology into global freight forwarding operations. The development, announced on October 26, 2026, introduces specialised AI agents capable of handling complex shipping tasks, including freight quotations, ocean booking requests and customs documentation. According to the company, its AI-powered pricing systems have already generated more than 80,000 freight quotations for over 3,600 customers, significantly reducing the time required to prepare international shipping offers. Quotations that previously took up to one day for air freight and two to three days for ocean shipments can now be completed in approximately two to three minutes. The expansion also introduces automated workflows for ocean bookings and customs processes, combining multiple AI agents to manage activities that traditionally required extensive manual coordination. AI agents transform freight pricing and ocean bookings C.H. Robinson’s new technology uses interconnected AI agents to evaluate shipment requirements, collect information from external sources and determine appropriate transportation options. Unlike its trucking operations, where a single AI agent can manage several freight pricing activities, ocean freight quotations require multiple agents working together to address the complexities of international shipping. These include identifying suitable origin and destination ports, evaluating terminal charges, assessing inland transportation options and determining appropriate shipping routes. The technology can also consider alternative transport modes, including road, rail and barge, alongside consolidation requirements for shipments moving through international supply chains. “As we’ve brought our AI playbook to global forwarding, the benefits keep compounding,” said Mike Short, President of Global Forwarding at C.H. Robinson. Short explained that faster access to shipping information enables customers to assess alternative routes, transport modes, schedules and pricing when disruptions or operational changes occur. The company’s AI-powered freight quotation capabilities were initially introduced in 2025 for less-than-container-load (LCL) ocean shipments involving customers in the United States and Canada. They have since expanded to full-container-load (FCL) ocean freight and air cargo, serving customers across Mexico, Europe, Latin America and Oceania. The technology is currently being piloted for customers in China, with further deployment planned across Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East and Africa during the fourth quarter of 2026. Ocean booking automation targets global rollout C.H. Robinson has also introduced AI agents designed to manage ocean booking requests, which the company receives in their thousands each week. The booking technology was launched in China in August 2026, with expansion across the rest of Asia planned during the fourth quarter. The company expects the system to become available globally during the first quarter of 2027. The agents process booking requests while incorporating customer-specific information, shipment requirements and operational preferences. Mike Neill, Chief Technology Officer at C.H. Robinson, said the company had previously achieved approximately 5% automation of ocean and air booking requests over roughly a decade using digital booking forms and customer data exchange systems. According to Neill, agentic AI offers an opportunity to automate more of these processes, particularly when shipment bookings originate from multiple suppliers rather than directly from customers. However, the company acknowledged that further development is required before every stage of the booking process can be automated. Customs automation reduces document processing time Beyond freight quotations and bookings, C.H. Robinson is applying AI to customs brokerage activities involving documentation required for shipments entering the United States. The company’s customs operations handle more than four dozen document types originating from shippers, carriers and government agencies. Its automated system classifies incoming documents, associates them with individual shipments and extracts relevant information. It also identifies missing documentation and initiates requests for the required materials. Additional automation supports the preparation of invoices and information packages once the relevant processes are completed. According to C.H. Robinson, these capabilities have reduced the time spent on the affected customs processing activities by 23%, allowing customs brokers to concentrate on validation and regulatory compliance. The company said its broader Lean AI strategy draws on hundreds of proprietary AI agents developed since 2023, supported by its internal engineering and data science teams. The latest expansion extends those capabilities into international freight forwarding, where pricing, carrier coordination, booking management and customs requirements involve multiple organisations and complex information flows. C.H. Robinson stated that human oversight remains part of its approach as it continues developing AI-driven processes across its global logistics operations.

articles.body: Business Developments & Projects October 26, 2026 · 7 hours ago Eni gets the ball rolling on execution of Mediterranean gas project Eni has kicked off the execution phase of Cyprus's 3 trillion cubic feet (tcf) gas project, targeting first production by H1 2028. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Map of the Cronos natural gas field development project in Block 6 offshore of Cyprus Source: TotalEnergies Italy’s energy giant Eni has fired the starting gun on the execution chapter of its Eastern Mediterranean project, awarding construction and drilling contracts to fast-track Cyprus's first-ever commercial gas development, which is expected to reach production of up to 500 million standard cubic feet per day (scf/d) in the first half of 2028, with gas to be processed and liquefied in Egypt before being shipped primarily to European markets. Eni has signed the main engineering, procurement, construction (EPC) and drilling contracts for the development of the Cronos project, marking the start of the project's execution phase and a key milestone towards the monetization of Cyprus' first gas development. According to the Italian giant, these contracts include floating control unit, transportation and installations, offshore seal lines, subsea production system, flexible lines, umbilicals, onshore line EPC, and drilling rig services. The contracting activity follows the final investment decision (FID) reached on July 28, 2026, for the development of the Cronos gas discovery in Block 6 offshore Cyprus. Related Articles Fossil Energy Cronos nexus unbound: Egypt and Cyprus put pen to paper for gas field development 3 min read With resources estimated at more than 3 tcf of gas initially in place, the project is expected to reach a production plateau of up to 500 million standard cubic feet per day, with start-up expected in H1 2028. The development will leverage a fast-track approach based on regional integration and the use of existing infrastructure. The execution phase was formally launched in Nicosia during a ceremony attended by Nikos Christodoulides , President of the Republic of Cyprus; Michael Damianos , Minister of Energy, Commerce, and Industry of the Republic of Cyprus; and Guido Brusco , Eni’s Chief Operating Officer of Global Natural Resources. Related Articles Fossil Energy Eni and TotalEnergies take FID for Cyprus’ first gas development 2 min read Gas produced from Cronos will be transported to Egypt, where it will be processed through existing facilities, including the Zohr infrastructure , before being liquefied at the Damietta LNG plant for export to international markets, primarily Europe. Block 6 is operated by Eni with a 50% interest, alongside its partner, TotalEnergies, which holds the remaining half. The Italian firm also operates Block 8 in Cyprus and holds participating interests in Blocks 7 and 11, which are operated by TotalEnergies. Eni highlighted: “As Eni's first development project in Cyprus and the country's first hydrocarbon development, Cronos represents a strategic milestone for the Republic of Cyprus. “The project will support the country's emergence as a natural gas producer and exporter while strengthening the integration of energy systems across the Eastern Mediterranean using existing Egyptian gas and LNG infrastructure.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: Reach Subsea, Eidesvik Complete Sale of Viking Reach Subsea Vessel
articles.summary: Reach Subsea and Eidesvik Offshore have completed the sale of the inspection, maintenance and repair (IMR) vessel Viking Reach, with the vessel delivered to its new owners on October 26.The transaction was completed through Eidesvik Reach, a joint venture between Reach Subsea and Eidesvik Offshore…
articles.body: Reach Subsea, Eidesvik Complete Sale of Viking Reach Subsea Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 Viking Reach (Credit: Eidesvik Offshore) Reach Subsea and Eidesvik Offshore have completed the sale of the inspection, maintenance and repair (IMR) vessel Viking Reach, with the vessel delivered to its new owners on October 26. The transaction was completed through Eidesvik Reach, a joint venture between Reach Subsea and Eidesvik Offshore, following a deal first announced in August 2026. Neither company identified the buyer in its latest announcement. Although not confirmed by October announcement, Asso Group reported on August 4 that it had signed a memorandum of agreement to acquire Viking Reach, along with a high-specification work-class remotely operated vehicle (WROV) spread, with completion initially expected in early fourth-quarter 2026. Built in 2009, the 85.3-meter-long Viking Reach is a DP-2 subsea IMR vessel equipped for subsea survey activities and a range of inspection, maintenance and repair operations. Under its previously announced plans, Asso Group intended to rename the vessel Arete, register it under the Greek flag and deploy it primarily as a trenching support vessel (TSV). The vessel is equipped with a 70-tonne active heave compensated (AHC) crane, integrated WROV and survey spreads, shallow-water capabilities and extensive deck space. Asso Group identified subsea cable protection, route preparation, post-lay burial and offshore wind projects among the vessel's intended applications. The acquisition agreement followed Asso Group's newbuild orders for the trenching support vessels Avra and Andromeda, as the company expands its capabilities in the subsea cable installation market.

articles.title: Why 25-year-old container ships are still commanding remarkable rates
articles.summary: The commercial value of ageing container ships is drawing renewed attention as recent charter agreements and second-hand vessel transactions demonstrate that ships approaching their third decade of service can still attract substantial financial commitments. According to the October 2026 edition of DynaLiners...
articles.body: The commercial value of ageing container ships is drawing renewed attention as recent charter agreements and second-hand vessel transactions demonstrate that ships approaching their third decade of service can still attract substantial financial commitments. According to the October 2026 edition of DynaLiners Monthly, several containerships built more than two decades ago have secured employment at significant daily rates, including contracts extending over multiple years. These fixtures, alongside recent transactions involving Euroseas, highlight how the economic value of older vessels can remain substantial despite their age. The developments raise an important question for container shipowners: when does continued employment become more attractive than selling an ageing vessel, particularly as new capacity continues to enter the global fleet? Ageing container ships continue to secure strong earnings A particularly revealing example is the EM Corfu , a 2,556 TEU feeder containership built in 2001 and owned by Euroseas. On 19 October 2026, Euroseas announced a new time charter agreement for the vessel at a gross daily rate of US$62,500, covering a minimum of 12 and a maximum of 14 months at the charterer’s option. The agreement is expected to begin in mid-December, following completion of the vessel’s scheduled dry-docking. The new rate represents a substantial increase from the US$28,000 per day agreed in November 2024 , when the company extended the vessel’s employment for 18–20 months. The difference between the two contracted daily rates amounts to approximately 123%. However, this comparison reflects the gross charter rates of separate agreements rather than an equivalent increase in operating profitability. Euroseas estimates that the latest charter will generate approximately US$17.8 million in EBITDA over its minimum contractual duration, illustrating the considerable earnings potential that an older feeder vessel can retain under favourable employment conditions. The broader charter market also provides examples of ageing container ships securing long-term employment commitments. According to DynaLiners, the 2001-built Cosco Hamburg , with a capacity of 5,400 TEU, was reported fixed to COSCO Shipping Lines at US$35,000 per day for 36 months. Another vessel, the 2002-built Algeciras Express , with a capacity of 4,300 TEU, was also reported chartered to COSCO Shipping Lines for 36 months at US$35,000 per day. Although differences in vessel specifications, operating capabilities and contractual arrangements limit direct comparisons, these transactions show that charterers continue to commit to older containerships for periods extending well beyond short-term employment. For owners, such agreements can provide greater visibility over future revenues. For charterers, they offer contractual access to capacity without requiring direct investment in vessel ownership. The choice between continued employment and vessel disposal For owners of ageing container ships, the economic considerations become particularly interesting when deciding whether to extend a vessel’s operational life or realise its value through a sale. Euroseas provides an example of these contrasting strategies through two sister vessels constructed in 2001. While the company secured a new charter for the EM Corfu , it also announced an agreement to sell the Evridiki G , another 2,556 TEU containership, for approximately US$26 million. The sale had not been completed at the time of the announcement. Euroseas stated that delivery to the unrelated buyer was expected following the completion of the vessel’s existing charter at the end of October 2026. The company anticipates recording a gain on the transaction of approximately US$22.5 million. These decisions illustrate two possible commercial outcomes for vessels of similar age and carrying capacity. One remains employed under a new charter agreement, while the other is expected to be sold. The distinction is important because charter revenue and second-hand asset values represent different financial considerations. A vessel generating substantial daily earnings may remain attractive to retain, particularly when its future employment is contractually secured. Conversely, a favourable sale price may encourage an owner to realise the asset’s value rather than incur additional expenditure associated with continued operation. However, the financial attractiveness of either strategy cannot be established through headline charter rates and sale prices alone. Operating expenses, maintenance requirements, financing costs, dry-docking expenditure and the vessel’s remaining useful life must also be considered. Special surveys become increasingly important For containerships approaching 25 years of age, major technical inspections and associated expenditure can become particularly influential in commercial decisions. This consideration was already evident in Euroseas’ November 2024 announcements involving the EM Corfu and Evridiki G . At the time, the company explained that the employment periods would extend towards the vessels’ fifth special surveys, when their economic prospects would be assessed against the costs of completing the required inspections and dry-docking. The subsequent October 2026 announcements provide a clear illustration of how different commercial decisions can emerge as ageing vessels approach these milestones. In the case of the EM Corfu , a new employment agreement is expected to begin after scheduled dry-docking. The Evridiki G , meanwhile, is expected to leave the Euroseas fleet through a sale. These developments do not establish that every ageing vessel is economically viable beyond its fifth special survey. They demonstrate, however, that commercial opportunities and technical expenditure must be assessed together rather than treating vessel age as the sole determining factor. Fleet expansion adds another dimension The commercial relevance of older tonnage must also be viewed against the continuing expansion of the global containership fleet. DynaLiners reports that 35 containerships, representing a combined 212,500 TEU, were delivered during the month preceding its October 2026 edition. Of these, 17 vessels exceeded 4,000 TEU, collectively accounting for 176,600 TEU of newly delivered capacity. The report identifies several major additions, including the 24,200 TEU CMA CGM Orsay , the 16,600 TEU Ever Eclat and the 16,200 TEU CMA CGM Alceste . These deliveries represent gross additions to the fleet rather than its net capacity growth, which also depends on factors such as vessel recycling and removals from service. The longer-term supply picture remains significant. As previously reported by Container News, citing BIMCO, global containership capacity was approaching 34 million TEU in September 2026, while nearly 2,000 vessels representing more than 5 million TEU were at least 20 years old. This ageing segment represents a substantial potential source of future recycling capacity, although the timing of vessel withdrawals remains uncertain. The relationship between newbuilding deliveries and older vessel employment is not straightforward. Large containerships and smaller feeder vessels serve different operational requirements, and capacity growth in one segment does not necessarily translate into equivalent competitive pressure across all vessel categories. Nevertheless, continued fleet expansion introduces a longer-term consideration for owners deciding whether to retain ageing tonnage. These developments also form part of the broader supply and demand dynamics examined in Container News’ container market analysis . Future earnings opportunities, operating efficiency, regulatory requirements and technical expenditure will all influence the commercial viability of older vessels as additional newbuildings enter service. Commercial value cannot be measured by age alone The latest fixtures and vessel transactions demonstrate that the economic relevance of a containership cannot be determined solely by its year of construction. The EM Corfu illustrates the potential for an older feeder vessel to secure significantly improved contractual earnings, while the agreed sale of the Evridiki G highlights the substantial asset value that an owner may be able to realise through disposal. Meanwhile, the longer-term charter agreements involving the Cosco Hamburg and Algeciras Express show that multi-year employment remains available for selected older vessels. These individual transactions should not be interpreted as proof that the entire ageing containership fleet is experiencing equivalent commercial conditions. They do, however, demonstrate that older vessels can remain economically relevant where suitable employment opportunities justify continued operation. As the global fleet expands and more containerships approach major technical and investment decisions, the balance between future charter earnings, maintenance expenditure and second-hand asset values will remain an important consideration for shipowners. For now, the latest reported transactions show that, even after 25 years of service, some containerships continue to command financial commitments that make their commercial future far from straightforward.

articles.title: MSC containership damaged after cruise ship collision in Bremerhaven
articles.summary: A TUI Cruises passenger vessel collided with two berthed containerships at the German port of Bremerhaven on 25 October, causing significant damage to one of the cargo vessels and prompting authorities to prohibit all three ships from departing. The incident occurred at approximately 17:30 local time, when the cruise...
articles.body: A TUI Cruises passenger vessel collided with two berthed containerships at the German port of Bremerhaven on 25 October, causing significant damage to one of the cargo vessels and prompting authorities to prohibit all three ships from departing. The incident occurred at approximately 17:30 local time, when the cruise ship Mein Schiff 3 was leaving Bremerhaven for a scheduled voyage to the Canary Islands. According to Bremen Police, the vessel was being assisted by tugboats when a strong gust of wind pushed it towards two containerships moored along the Stromkaje quay. One of the vessels involved has been identified in maritime industry reports as the 16,520 TEU MSC Victorine . The second containership was also struck during the incident. Significant damage reported to containership In an updated statement issued on 26 October, Bremen Police confirmed that the larger containership sustained substantial structural damage, while the smaller vessel suffered minor damage. The collision tore open several metres of the larger containership’s port-side hull and deformed container guides. Police said the damaged sections were several metres above the waterline, and no water ingress was reported on any of the three vessels. The Mein Schiff 3 also sustained considerable damage, including to its lifeboats, associated launching equipment and exterior hull. Despite the severity of the collision, no injuries were reported. According to information provided by TUI Cruises to German media, the cruise ship was carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members at the time. Authorities prohibit departure of all three vessels Following the incident, Mein Schiff 3 abandoned its planned voyage and returned to the cruise terminal in Bremerhaven. Bremen Police confirmed that the maritime safety authority imposed a departure ban on all three vessels involved in the collision. The restrictions were introduced following assessments of the damage sustained during the incident. TUI Cruises subsequently cancelled the planned Canary Islands voyage after inspections identified damage requiring urgent shipyard repairs. The Bremen Water Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances of the collision. No timetable has been confirmed for the affected containerships to resume operations.

articles.title: CM Technologies Raises Alarm Over Recent Shipping Fuel Quality Concerns
articles.summary: German testing specialist CM Technologies (CMT) advises that shipowners and operators need to maintain close checks on fuel quality following a series of off-specification alerts at major bunkering ports and warns that contaminated or unstable…
articles.body: CM Technologies Raises Alarm Over Recent Shipping Fuel Quality Concerns Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © CM Technologies German testing specialist CM Technologies (CMT) advises that shipowners and operators need to maintain close checks on fuel quality following a series of off-specification alerts at major bunkering ports and warns that contaminated or unstable fuels can result in costly engine damage and vessel downtime. The advisory follows reports of fuel quality problems at Antwerp, Rotterdam, Houston, Singapore, Hong Kong, Piraeus and other bunkering locations during the past six months, involving excessive catalytic fines, poor fuel stability, high sediment levels and low flash points. In part, the drop in fuel quality can be attributed to the supply chain disruption caused by the current geopolitical landscape and conflict, said David Fuhlbrügge, joint managing director at CM Technologies (CMT). In August, fuel testing specialist VPS identified the Middle East conflict as a major factor behind both rising bunker prices and deteriorating fuel quality. It also issued 29 bunker alerts during the first seven months of 2026, with excessive catalytic fines and fuel stability problems accounting for 72% of them. Data published by West P&I in September, covering fuel samples tested between April and September 2026, found technical off-specification rates for heavy fuel oil (HFO) of 46.2% in Antwerp, 41.4% in Norfolk, 38% in the Panama Canal region and 35.5% in Rotterdam. The same report identified elevated sulphur off-specification rates among very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) samples tested in Rotterdam and Antwerp, although the club cautioned that the sample populations were comparatively small. Fuhlbrügge said the findings reinforced the need for shipmanagers to remain vigilant over the quality of fuels taken onboard, irrespective of the bunkering location. "Fuel quality should never be taken for granted. The consequences of getting it wrong can be expensive, not only in terms of machinery repairs but also the time spent dealing with blocked filters, damaged components and interrupted operations." In July, alerts were also published concerning high abrasive content in HFO supplied in Houston and the Amsterdam–Rotterdam–Antwerp region, severe fuel stability concerns in Piraeus, high sediment in Las Palmas and low flash point fuels in Hong Kong and Singapore. “Catalytic fines are particularly damaging if they are not adequately removed during fuel treatment. The abrasive particles can accelerate wear in fuel injection equipment, cylinder liners and piston rings, potentially shortening component life and increasing maintenance requirements,” said Fuhlbrügge. Fuhlbrügge added that the risks do not necessarily end once a bunker delivery had passed its initial laboratory checks. "Shipowners need to know how the fuel will behave once it is onboard, particularly when different batches are stored or mixed. Two fuels may be stable individually but incompatible when combined. Finding that out after sludge has formed in the tanks can mean considerable cleaning work and avoidable expense." The commercial consequences are reflected in claims data from marine insurer Gard, which handled more than 70 bunker-related claims between January and May 2026, an increase of 50% over the corresponding period last year. Almost all involved fuel quality, with some vessels disabled or requiring towage. Lloyd's Register FOBAS has also suggested that fuels meeting routine ISO 8217 specifications can still cause operational problems, particularly where unusual blending components or poor compatibility affect fuel handling and treatment. CMT supplies onboard test equipment for checking fuel compatibility, catalytic fines, water content, viscosity and density. Its compatibility tester, for example, allows engineers to assess the behavior of different fuel batches before mixing, while its other instruments provide additional checks on fuel condition.

articles.title: Stena AB to Acquire Shipping Company Color Line
articles.summary: The Swedish industrial Group Stena AB, owner of ferry operator Stena Line, has entered into an agreement to acquire the Norwegian shipping company Color Line, subject to regulatory approval. The transaction will bring together two companies…
articles.body: Stena AB to Acquire Shipping Company Color Line Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © Color Line The Swedish industrial Group Stena AB, owner of ferry operator Stena Line, has entered into an agreement to acquire the Norwegian shipping company Color Line, subject to regulatory approval. The transaction will bring together two companies with complementary operations in European passenger and freight transport, creating added value and benefits for both companies’ customers. Following completion, Stena intends for Color Line to continue as a separate, independent business and brand, with local management in Norway and Norwegian-registered ships. At the same time, Stena will use its industrial expertise, reach and experience to strengthen and further develop Color Line, including in decarbonization, technology and digitalization, customer service and logistics. The signing of the agreement will not affect sailings, bookings or ongoing customer and supplier relationships within Color Line or Stena-owned Stena Line. Both companies will continue to operate as separate, independent businesses while the transaction awaits regulatory approval. The transaction will be structured as a share purchase agreement under which Stena AB’s wholly owned subsidiary, Stena Rederi AB acquires all shares in Color Group AS from ONS Invest II AS, which is wholly owned by Olav Nils Sunde and his family. ONS Invest II owns 100% of Color Group, which in turn owns 100% of Color Line and its subsidiaries. The parties have agreed not to disclose the value of the proposed transaction, which is subject to regulatory review. The proposed transaction is expected to be completed towards the end of Q1 or during Q2 2027.

Caddell II Continues as Chairman Caddell Dry Dock & Repair Co., Inc. has announced a planned executive leadership transition effective January 1, 2027, marking the next chapter for the longstanding New York Harbor ship repair company while maintaining continuity in its ownership and strategic direction. Salvatore Molino, currently Executive Vice President, will become President of Caddell Dry Dock & Repair Co., Inc . , succeeding Steven Kalil, who will transition to Chief Executive Officer after 36 years as President. William Chapman will continue to serve as Vice President and General Manager, and Ciro Galeno, Jr. will continue to serve as Secretary and Treasurer. John B. Caddell II will remain Chairman of the Board, continuing his longstanding stewardship of the privately held company and its commitment to investment in its people, facilities and ship repair capabilities: “Our responsibility is to build a company that is prepared not only for the work in front of us today, but for the opportunities and challenges that will come decades from now. That philosophy has guided our investment in Caddell, our people and our facilities, and it is the same philosophy behind this succession plan.” “Steve has dedicated decades to building this company and strengthening its position in the maritime industry. Salvatore has demonstrated the leadership and vision needed to carry that work forward. With Steve moving into the CEO role and Salvatore becoming President, we are putting in place a leadership structure designed to protect what Caddell’s has built while positioning the company for its future.” The succession represents a deliberate evolution of Caddell’s leadership structure following years of investment in the business and long-term planning intended to position Caddell for continued growth while preserving the independence, workforce and operating principles that have defined the company for generations. Kalil Moves to CEO After 36 Years as President “After 36 years as President, what I am most proud of is not simply what we have built, but the people who built it,” Kalil said. “Caddell’s reputation comes from generations of skilled men and women who understand this business and take pride in the vessels we repair.” “The best succession plans preserve that experience while creating room for the next generation of leadership to move the company forward. John’s continued commitment to investing in Caddell gives us that stability. Salvatore understands our operation, our customers and where this industry is headed. I have tremendous confidence in his ability to lead Caddell as President.” Molino to Assume Presidency Kalil’s tenure as President has spanned more than three decades of change across the commercial maritime, government vessel and ship repair sectors. During that period, he has helped guide Caddell’s development in the New York Harbor market while building longstanding relationships with customers, employees and industry partners. As CEO, Kalil will remain actively involved in Caddell’s strategic direction, business development, major customer and industry relationships, long-term planning and corporate initiatives. “After 36 years as President, what I am most proud of is not simply what we have built, but the people who built it,” Kalil said. “Caddell’s reputation comes from generations of skilled men and women who understand this business and take pride in the vessels we repair.” “The best succession plans preserve that experience while creating room for the next generation of leadership to move the company forward. John’s continued commitment to investing in Caddell gives us that stability. Salvatore understands our operation, our customers and where this industry is headed. I have tremendous confidence in his ability to lead Caddell as President.” Molino to Assume Presidency Molino joined Caddell’s executive leadership team as Executive Vice President in 2022 and has worked closely with Caddell and Kalil on operational performance, strategic growth, customer relationships, competitive positioning, facility development and long-term corporate initiatives. As President, Molino will assume responsibility for Caddell’s day-to-day executive leadership, operations and organizational performance while working with Kalil and the company’s management team to execute its long-term strategy. “It is an extraordinary privilege to be entrusted with the leadership of a company that has been part of New York Harbor’s maritime community for generations,” Molino said. “Our job now is to build on that foundation. We will continue investing in our workforce, infrastructure and capabilities while finding new ways to serve our commercial and government customers. We intend to grow, but we will do it without losing the craftsmanship, responsiveness and accountability that built Caddell’s reputation in the first place.” Positioning Caddell for the Next Generation The leadership transition comes as Caddell continues to evaluate investments aimed at expanding its repair and dry dock capabilities and strengthening its ability to support commercial and government vessels operating in New York Harbor and beyond. For Molino, continued investment in both infrastructure and skilled trades will be central to maintaining Caddell’s competitiveness. “Ship repair remains a people-and-infrastructure business,” Molino said. “You need the waterfront assets and equipment to handle the vessel, but ultimately, it is experienced people who deliver the project. Our future depends on investing in both.” “New York Harbor remains one of the most important maritime gateways in the country, and we believe there is significant opportunity for a shipyard that can combine experience with continued investment and modernization. Our objective is to make sure Caddell is positioned to meet that opportunity for decades to come.” Effective January 1, 2027 , Caddell’s executive leadership structure will be: John B. articles.title: DP World Converts Ghost Nets Into Sunglasses
articles.summary: DP World is working with Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Türkiye’s Marine Life Conservation Society) to remove ghost nets from the Sea of Marmara and give the recovered material a second life. Ghost nets can take up to 200 years to degrade, and left under the waves…
articles.body: DP World Converts Ghost Nets Into Sunglasses Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © DP World © DP World DP World is working with Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği (Türkiye’s Marine Life Conservation Society) to remove ghost nets from the Sea of Marmara and give the recovered material a second life. Ghost nets can take up to 200 years to degrade, and left under the waves, they continue to trap and kill marine life, from sharks and turtles to much smaller organisms, long after they have been lost or abandoned. The project aims to remove more than 1,000 m² of nets from the seabed around the Princes’ Islands, or about 800 kg of material. The Deniz Yaşamını Koruma Derneği team tracks down abandoned nets using reports, technology, sea charts and local knowledge before carefully retrieving them from the seabed. The weight, size and location of each net are recorded, helping to build a clearer picture of where lost fishing gear has accumulated. The work is focused in particular on deeper waters around Istanbul and the Princes’ Islands. Some of the nets have been recovered from more than 50 meters below the surface, including one found at a depth of 55 meters around the Princes’ Islands. During one recovery operation, the team also found three ray egg cases among the material brought to the surface. The egg cases were returned to the sea as soon as they were discovered. Once back on land, the nets begin their transformation. They are processed into recycled plastic granules and turned into custom-designed sunglasses, giving material that once threatened marine life new, longer-lasting use. Each pair has its own story. The coordinates and depth where the original net was found are stamped inside the frames, creating a direct link back to the waters it came from. Not all the recovered material will become sunglasses. DP World is also working with SUSAKO, the Sustainable Art Women’s Cooperative (Sürdürülebilir Sanat Kadın Kooperatifi). Together, they will run workshops where members of the public can turn ghost-net plastic into jewelery, showing how something once considered waste can be repurposed, while supporting women’s participation in the economy. The project will also work with fishing communities to raise awareness of ghost nets and help prevent fishing gear from being lost or abandoned in the first place.

articles.title: Black Sea Shipping Faces Insurance Squeeze as Constanta Port Stays Resilient
articles.summary: Shipping through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta was stable and grain exports had increased by end-September, the port authority said, despite a spike in marine insurance premiums driven by increased attacks on cargo vessels.In September…
articles.body: Black Sea Shipping Faces Insurance Squeeze as Constanta Port Stays Resilient Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 26, 2026 © hecke71 / Adobe Stock Shipping through Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta was stable and grain exports had increased by end-September, the port authority said, despite a spike in marine insurance premiums driven by increased attacks on cargo vessels. In September, London's marine insurance market widened the area in the Black Sea it lists as high risk, as Russia's war in Ukraine escalated, with only the territorial waters of Georgia, Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey exempted. The Black Sea is a vital route for grain, crude oil and refined products and the four countries share its waters alongside Ukraine and Russia. However, the past three weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least eight cargo ships hit and some 34 sailors reported dead or missing. The Constanta port authority told Reuters the total volume of goods shipped through the port by end-September stood at 51.55 million tons, virtually unchanged from the same period of 2025. The data predates the October attacks. Grain exports through the port – one of the European Union's largest grain shipping centres – totaled 15.8 million metric tons, up 7% from a year earlier. Ukrainian grain exports through Constanta had also risen to 1.03 million tons compared with 321,000 tons in the first nine months of 2025. The port authority will release figures for this month in November. The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards Romania's Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is the primary export route for Ukraine, one of t he world's biggest grain and food oil exporters. Although ships calling at Constanta port are not targeted, overall Black Sea risks had pushed up insurance premiums. "Insurance is available," a source in the London insurance market told Reuters. "It is expensive because of the attacks and a few insurers are shying away. "But (ship) owners can still get coverage for (the) Romania Black Sea, there's no withdrawal of capacity." (Reuters - Reporting by Luiza Ilie; Editing by David Holmes)

articles.title: Tight reservoirs on Equinor and Aker BP’s agenda amid Norway’s 2.8-billion-boe potential
articles.summary: Equinor and Aker BP have joined forces to unlock the recovery potential of tight oil and gas reservoirs on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS).
articles.body: Exploration & Production October 26, 2026 · 9 hours ago Tight reservoirs on Equinor and Aker BP’s agenda amid Norway’s 2.8-billion-boe potential Equinor and Aker BP have joined forces to unlock the recovery potential of tight oil and gas reservoirs on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS). MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Credit: Lone Stormoen/Equinor Norwegian energy heavyweights Equinor and Aker BP are pooling their expertise and portfolios to accelerate technology development and improve the commercial viability of tight-reservoir discoveries on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, where estimated recovery potential amounts to around 2.8 billion barrels of oil equivalent (boe). Equinor and Aker BP are entering into a strategic collaboration on tight reservoirs on the NCS, with the aim of enabling the profitable development of more discoveries and increasing the oil and gas recovery rate through technology development, standardization, and cooperation across multiple projects. The Norwegian Offshore Directorate has estimated a recovery potential of around 2.8 billion barrels of oil equivalent in mapped tight reservoirs, which is believed to be comparable to the expected recoverable resources in the Johan Sverdrup field. These are reservoirs where oil and gas flow very slowly through the rock. Kjetil Hove , Equinor’s Executive Vice President for Exploration & Production Norway, emphasized: “By viewing our portfolios in context and developing common solutions, we can reduce costs and develop and qualify technology faster. Together, we can make challenging resources profitable. This benefits all partners and society at large.” Flow of oil and gas in conventional and tight reservoirs; Source: Equinor Given that large volumes of oil and gas are found in tight reservoirs on the NCS, the Norwegian Offshore Directorate has encouraged the companies to increase collaboration on technology, standardization, and knowledge sharing. Equinor emphasizes that many of the approximately 90 discoveries that have yet to receive development approval are in tight reservoirs, while only a limited amount of these resources can be recovered using conventional methods, with many discoveries being too costly to develop using current solutions. Karl Johnny Hersvik , Chief Executive Officer of Aker BP, underlined: “Scale is key. By considering the opportunities across both portfolios together, we can create basis for activity, faster learning and lower costs. Together, we can develop solutions that can be applied across multiple projects. We are starting the work immediately.” Related Articles Fossil Energy Cooperation, cost cuts, and new tech keys to unlock oil & gas from tight reservoirs 3 min read Aker BP and Equinor’s collaboration covers prospects, discoveries, and projects across the NCS, with the duo contributing relevant opportunities from their own portfolios and identifying where joint technology development, standardization, and knowledge sharing can create the greatest value. This pact also includes resource maturation and solutions for well stimulation, with the ambition to create a sufficient and predictable level of activity to build a competitive value chain, with the expertise and supplier capacity needed to develop more discoveries in tight reservoirs. The collaboration will be organized through a joint governance structure and multidisciplinary working groups with participants from both companies. The Norwegian Offshore Directorate estimated in 2019 that mapped tight reservoirs contain 12–13 billion barrels of oil and gas in place. However, the recovery rate is low. The Norwegian government agency estimates an average recovery rate of 20% (5–40%) for oil and 30% (10–50%) for gas in limestone reservoirs, while the average recovery rate has been estimated at 12% (4–20%) for oil and 25% (18–40%) for gas in sandstone reservoirs. “The companies will contribute relevant opportunities from their respective portfolios and jointly identify where technology development, standardization and exchange of experience can create the greatest value,” underlined Aker BP. The UAE said on Friday that efforts were under way to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. Authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill. But experts told Reuters that the spill was coming from a tanker called the Gem No.2, which shipping sources said was a vessel that had been struck by an unidentified projectile last month, causing a fire that was later extinguished. The images provided by the EU’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites showed a large oil spill coming from the tanker. Authorities across various northern emirates responded to the spill by restricting access to coastal areas. The Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday that all beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed, while authorities in neighboring Sharjah shut access to Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution. “The reported oil spill off Umm Al Quwain is a serious environmental concern. The temporary closure of beaches and coastal areas is a prudent precaution while the extent of the spill and the movement of the oil are assessed,” Nidal Hilal, Professor of Engineering and Director of New York University Abu Dhabi’s Water Research Center, told Reuters. In Ras Al Khaimah, known for its beaches and luxury resorts, authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice. The UAE’s marine life “is rich in fish, plants and corals, with over 500 different species of fish inhabiting the Gulf waters,” including dolphins and marine turtles, the International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, says on its website. (Source: Ansgar Walk) By Thomas Seal Oct 26, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Dubai’s DP World Ltd. is set to unveil a deal backing potential development of Canada’s port of Churchill, a northern outpost that Prime Minister Mark Carney aims to expand for exports to Europe and other markets. The global port operator has negotiated a memorandum of understanding with two Canadian entities, including Arctic Gateway Group, the owner and operator of the Churchill port and an associated railway, according to two people familiar with the matter who requested they not be identified. The agreement focuses on port operations and a possible transportation corridor to link Churchill with DP World’s global logistics network and inland port facilities managed by CentrePort Canada Inc. Churchill is a remote town in the north of the Canadian province of Manitoba. It sits on Hudson Bay, which connects to the Atlantic Ocean via Arctic waterways. Its location means that it could someday become a gateway to ship Canadian resources like liquefied natural gas, grain, potash and other critical minerals to customers in the Middle East and Europe. But doing all of that would take tens of billions of dollars of investment. Canada and the United Arab Emirates have been developing closer economic ties since Carney came to office last year with an agenda to build his country’s trade and investment connections with the rest of the world after US President Donald Trump started a trade war. Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan, the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, is scheduled to visit Ottawa on Monday and Tuesday, Carney’s office announced on Sunday. Last year, the UAE committed to invest C$70 billion ($49.9 billion) in Canada. “At a time of profound global transformation, Canada and the UAE are working to deepen their partnership and build greater economic strength, shared security, and long-term prosperity for people in both countries,” Carney’s office said . Canadian Energy Minister Tim Hodgson told Bloomberg News last year that Churchill has “tremendous potential” as a much larger export hub. The bay is currently frozen for most of the year, but Hodgson said it could be opened up for extended shipping seasons with icebreakers. Canada signed a deal for new ice-breaking ships in August. Read More: Canada Eyes Arctic Ocean Port to Ship Gas, Commodities to Europe Discussions about the port advanced during September meetings between UAE officials and Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew at the time of the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto in mid-September. A prospectus shared by Canada’s government with summit attendees put the price tag of a major expansion of Churchill and supporting infrastructure at $57 billion, with “preliminary investment requests” of $3.9 billion. That pitchbook said the initiative is to turn Churchill “into a four-season trade gateway through an LNG export corridor, rail upgrades, port modernization, and develop all-weather road access.” DP World already has extensive interests in Canada. It currently operates the container port in Prince Rupert on Canada’s west coast, and last year won the contract to operate a new terminal near Montreal. articles.title: Rig sinking incident: Search continues for five missing as 'robust' probe looms
articles.summary: Borr Drilling has emphasized that search and rescue mission for five offshore workers that are still missing remains the “overriding priority.”
articles.body: Human Capital October 26, 2026 · 11 hours ago Rig sinking incident: Search continues for five missing as 'robust' probe looms Borr Drilling has emphasized that search and rescue mission for five offshore workers that are still missing remains the “overriding priority.” MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Prospector 5 jack-up rig Source: Borr Drilling As search and rescue crews continue to comb the waters off the coast of Gabon for five missing personnel following the sinking of a 2014-built jack-up rig, Bermuda-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Borr Drilling has confirmed that 110 of the 115 people on board have been safely accounted for and brought ashore, while assuring that a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident will be conducted to determine how this tragedy unfolded. The rig owner’s 2014-built Prospector 5 rig experienced a punch through event at approximately 20:37 local time on October 24, 2026, during preload activities, resulting in loss of stability and the subsequent sinking of the rig, based on preliminary information. The rig was conducting jacking operations offshore Gabon at the time of the incident in preparation for a planned campaign to support BW Energy 's drilling operations at the Dussafu license . Related Articles Safety Rig incident: 110 rescued, 5 still missing after Borr Drilling’s jack-up sinks off Gabon coast 2 min read In an update on October 26, Borr Drilling emphasized that out of the 115 personnel on board during the rig incident, 110 were safe and accounted for. These workers are being brought ashore in Gabon, where care and support is being provided. “Search and rescue operations are ongoing for the five individuals who remain unaccounted for. The company is in contact with the families of the missing personnel,” added the rig owner. Borr Drilling highlights that its onshore emergency response team continues to work with local authorities and BW Energy to respond to the incident, support those affected, and continue to search for missing personnel, as extensive marine and air search and rescue operations remain ongoing. The firm underlined: “The company is working with its partners and authorities to ensure a robust investigation is carried out into the cause of the incident; however, the immediate and overriding priority remains the ongoing search and rescue efforts and doing everything possible to assist the authorities and specialists leading these operations to locate the missing individuals and support those safely accounted for.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go!
